Before I continue with some remarks on that subject, I should like to make this observation. I should like nothing that is being said today by way of recommendations that we might be willing to back as a party to be construed in any shape or form by our political enemies or by the communists in Canada as anything in the nature of aggressive intent. For anyone to consider that Canada might at any time be aggressive or that our defence policies might be so directed would be utterly ridiculous. We are a country of twelve million people. Mr. Chairman, on a question of privilege, could we have more order?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

Once again I should like to ask all hon. members to deal specif -


ically with the item before the committee. If the item were for administration, there could be a general discussion of the activities of the department, but in dealing with this specific item I hope the members will not go beyond it.
In this item there is mention of future commitments for the R.C.A.F.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

It is for $19 million odd. From
the time I first came into this house I have urged that Canada's defence policy should aim at the development of fighter planes capable of meeting any aggressive action that can be taken against our country. I intend to speak on that again today, because the vote involves a future commitment, and we are already aware of the fact that the government has under consideration the manufacture of fighter planes in Canada of a type now manufactured in the United States.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

speechtext: Yes-future commitments. I am recommending to the government that its policy be so directed that it will develop in Canada a fighter force capable of defending this country and the people in it. Sweden, which is a country about half the size of Canada, has a modern fighter force. The Swedes are a peace-loving people, just as we are. They have no aggressive intent anywhere, but they have a fighter force of 300 modern machines.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I would ask the hon. member to confine his remarks to the item before the committee. This has nothing to do with Sweden. It is a well-known rule that remarks made in committee must be relevant to the item under discussion, and I would ask hon. members to observe the rule.
I was just endeavouring to make a comparison between the defence of Canada and the defence of Sweden. I think it is in order to give to the minister a comparison.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I want to say this in all kindliness to my hon. friend. It is not in order, in the consideration of a specific item in the estimates of the Department of National Defence, to talk about Sweden or other countries.

The last thing I want to do, Mr. Chairman, is to engage in a controversy with you. But I humbly submit to you as chairman of this committee that when the item says "to authorize further commitments for future years", what I am doing is completely in order.
The Depuiy Chairman: Speeches in committee must be strictly relevant to the item under consideration. I should like the hon. member to tell the Chair and the committee what this item has to do with Sweden or any other country.

I can tell you, sir, in just a few words. Future commitments with regard to the Royal Canadian Air Force have to do with the type of aircraft used and the type of expenditure made by this department. They have to do with the question whether the people of Canada will be assured of adequate measures for defence. We know at the moment that there are only about seventy-five modern fighting machines in Canada. With the hundreds of millions of dollars that have been spent since the war, our country has only seventy-five Vampires-the only modern fighting machine in Canada. My remarks are directed toward the government to the end that their future commitments will be more intelligent than they have been in the past.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: What has this to do with Sweden or any other place? It is not in order.

Then, Mr. Chairman, may I say that a country half the size of Canada has a fighter force three times the size of the one that our country has at the moment, and by the end of this year it will have one that is ten times the size of Canada's.
These remarks are all directed toward this thought which was expressed so well by Ovid's "Tristia", where these words are found:
The robber and the wary traveler are both girded with swords; but the one carries his for outrage, the other for self-defence.
I am advocating that Canada be girded with a sword as a wary traveler in order that it will be able to defend itself. I am saying here today that unless this country has a modern fighter force and the organization to back it up, the minister can never make another speech in which he tells the Canadian people that he is defending this country, because it cannot be. We cannot have an effective army, an effective navy, or effective defence unless the first line is held properly, and that with a fighter defence force in Canada.
Yesterday we had under discussion the question of North Star aircraft, and I want
Supply-National Defence to direct a few remarks to this matter, as it is part of the question of future commitments so far as Canada is concerned. There is a question whether the R.C.A.F. ever needed these aircraft. There is a question whether it ever asked for them. There is a question whether more than half of them have ever been in service at the same time. If we were privileged to have in this country a defence committee, I feel that the examination of those three questions would be an important matter; that it would be in the country's interest to have the minister produce the actual requisition from the R.C.A.F. for North Star aircraft, and, against that, the reasons why they were asked for.
We know that at the close of hostilities we had a surplus of various kinds of aircraft in Canada, and suddenly there appeared in their midst twenty to twenty-four new North Star aircraft. I am not discussing the merits of the machine as a passenger aircraft; I hear it is a good one. Although they have had some initial difficulties, I understand those are being overcome. That is not the point, however. The point is that Canada needs a fighter force, and has twenty-four transport passenger aircraft handed to it by the government. It is important for the country to know whether the minister receives aircraft from the Canadian factories for the R.C.A.F., or whether the R.CA.F. pays for these aircraft without a proper requisition being made for them, without actually a need having been shown for that type of machine in the defence of our country.
We also know that six of those North Star aircraft were immediately lent to T.C.A. As soon as they were manufactured they went on loan to T.C.A., and they were placed on the north Atlantic run to the United Kingdom, where I understand they have been flown almost to exhaustion and then handed back to the R.C.A.F. It would be interesting to know whether T.C.A. paid the cost of reconditioning them and putting them back in proper order, or whether the air force had to do this; or whether when they were returned to the air force they were in shape to fly should the air force wish to fly them, or should they be allocated to the active part of the minister's reserve.
I think these are questions that the country should have answered. It is only too easy for these things to get caught between two departments, and we might find that the R.C.A.F. actually paid for those machines which were flown to exhaustion by T.C.A., and possibly they were returned to them unreconditioned. I am merely putting that proposition forward as an example of what

Supply-National Defence could happen under this type of organization, and I would appreciate the minister's comments.
To return to the defence of Canada, which is what we are really talking about when we talk about future commitments: On this continent we are in the same position today as Great Britain was in the thirties. They had a defence problem, and they formed a policy as early as 1935. That policy was the same as the one I am advocating today, namely, that a fighter defence force has to be maintained in order to meet any initial aggression against Canada.
It is interesting to note that back in 1935 and 1936 the air ministry in Great Britain anticipated the battle of Britain and its importance to that country, although that battle was not to be fought for five long years. Their plans were laid. The Spitfire and the Hurricane were then under development, and arrived in time for that battle. Our condition today on the North American continent is exactly similar to the condition in the United Kingdom at that time. I believe that we should take the first essential step, the development of our defence forces, as they did at that time. I have made that suggestion before in the house, and I do it again. I believe that is the first task in Canadian defence.
As recently as a year ago the minister said that Canada must ensure positive security under her own arms. He made that statement in Montreal in February, 1948. I wonder whether we have made any progress. I hope we have.
Again at a meeting of the young men's board of trade on May 4, 1948, the minister said:
Our job will be to supply the minimum quantity of interceptors and the ground forces to deal with local attacks, as well as to develop the staff and personnel to take their place as part of any major striking forces.
He said in that speech in Montreal before the young men's board of trade that we should supply the minimum quantity of interceptors. We certainly have the minimum in Canada; there is no doubt about that. We wonder how many of the seventy-five Vampires which are left are efficient, and how many of them are effective; whether in fact they are not being cannibalized for spare parts, and slowly but surely so handled that they are being reduced to a mere handful. Hon. members know what "cannibalize" means so far as aircraft are concerned. It means that those which are working are living off the others. Those in the hangars are giving their spare parts-new wing sections, tailplanes and the like, to keep them serviceable. That means that if you buy

fifty machines you probably have the use of five of them to produce spare parts, and you really have a force of forty-five instead of the fifty which you paid for.
In Canada we are being asked to trust the government in a great many ways so far as defence is concerned. We are being asked to permit the minister to remain silent on points which we consider to be essential to security. For that reason a committee in camera is absolutely necessary in order that hon. members may be properly informed as to the state of Canada's defences. We know that they are not good.
It is four years since the end of hostilities. We have had all that time to develop, to make an appreciation of what the future will require for this country. We joined the United Nations, which committed our country to joint efforts to resist aggression. We joined the Atlantic pact, but can we do anything about it? Are we just a silent partner of these other nations, or are we to make a contribution? I believe that the people of Canada want our government and parliament to see to it that a proper contribution is made towards collective security against aggression. Unless the minister can so direct his departments, particularly the air department, as to be able to make that contribution, unless he is able to achieve that, he should hand his resignation to the Prime Minister of Canada and let somebody take over who can.

Mr. Chairman, there is one matter I should like to place briefly before the Minister of National Defence. It arises out of a newspaper dispatch which appeared on Monday of this week, reading as follows: Pacific pact to be discussed in Ottawa talks
A Pacific defence pact to buttress Canada's western approaches-as the North Atlantic treaty had secured the east-was "definitely on the agenda" in scheduled talks between Australian Defence Minister Sir Frederick Shedden and Defence Minister Claxton.
Sir Frederick had been invited to the United States to discuss joint problems, and a similar invitation had been issued by Canada's defence department.
The dispatch went on to give the view of the Canadian defence department with regard to this pact, and then follows the part about which I am particularly concerned. It reads:
By the defence department, possible Pacific pact proposals were regarded as the "United States' baby." Canada was "not going to take the initiative" in proposing a defence barrier against aggression from the East.
And the article concluded by saying that the problem of mutual defence would be the main substance of the talks, which might "very possibly" pave the way for Pacific pact discussion.
For those Canadians who live on the Pacific slope this question of a Pacific defence pact is of great concern, as I believe it is also of concern to Canadians in other parts of the country. I realize that the minister himself visited Australia just a year or two ago, and

Supply-National Defence no doubt is closely in touch with this whole picture. Unfortunately the threat to freedom today is not confined to Europe and the north Atlantic. It may be that in that area the soviet is already well contained. In Asia, however, the soviet is going ahead by leaps and bounds. There are communist armies swarming over China; a greatly increased communist vote in Japan; communist uprisings in Malaya and in Burma, and a communist problem in India. In fact in that part of the world it looks as though the soviet is winning by default.
Is this kind of debate in order on this item, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I understand the hon.
member is discussing this item in relation to Pacific defence. That is what occurred to me.

As I was saying, it looks as though in Asia the soviet is winning by default. It may be that while we are bolting the front door by the North Atlantic treaty, we are leaving the back door open by doing nothing in the Pacific. Winston Churchill summed up that situation in his speech on April 1, when he said:
Whether the western democracies are winning the cold war cannot be decided by looking at Europe alone, he said.
"We must also look at Asia. The worst disaster since our victory has been the collapse of China under communist attack and intrigue. China, in which the United States has always taken a high interest, comprises an immense part of the population of the world. The absorption of China and India into the Kremlin-controlled communist empire would certainly bring measureless bloodshed and misery to eight or nine hundred million people. On the other hand," Churchill said, "the position in Europe has so far been successfully maintained."
That affects Canada directly, and particularly western Canada; because if trouble comes it may come from the Pacific. If it did, I suggest that Canada would be the centre of the fighting. The easiest way for soviet forces to get at the production centres of Canada and the United States would be by coming across Behring strait to Alaska, on into Yukon and then down to Edmonton. As a matter of fact I believe many soviet airmen flew that route during the war, when they operated the planes the Americans were supplying to the soviet, going in the other direction across Behring strait. This is also the gateway to British Columbia and to the Northwest Territories, where our deposits of uranium are found; and of course uranium is one of the vital strategic materials on this continent.
I believe Canada is so directly affected by what goes on in the Pacific area that she should be taking the lead in advocating a Pacific defence pact. It would include most

of the nations already in the North Atlantic pact, as for example the United States, the United Kingdom, France and the Netherlands, all of which are involved in the Pacific as well. But it would include also our old friends Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, India, Pakistan, Ceylon and the Philippines; a Pacific defence pact would fill the gap at present existing in that area. There is one other reason for a Pacific defence pact.

I should hope that while the Australian minister of defence is here some such arrangement could be made. Would the minister be prepared to give a statement on this question?
It is not my purpose or intention, Mr. Chairman, to delay for an instant the progress of this committee.
Oh, oh.
But I am going to challenge my hon. friends opposite. I find myself terribly confused.
Oh, oh.

If you are conscious of your responsibilities as members of this house I am sure you too must ask yourselves many questions at this time. It must be remembered that a few days ago the leader of the opposition directed certain questions to the Minister of National Defence, to which he received certain replies. Let us not fool ourselves. Yesterday in this very chamber the minister had ample opportunity to rise on a question of privilege; indeed, he spoke at considerable length in committee, but failed to correct the false impression he left with the members of this house. So having regard to my responsibility to the people of Canada, particularly those of my own constituency, when I am asked to pass an item of more than $19 million for national defence, I think I am entitled to know upon whose advice I can depend. Through the signing of the Atlantic pact undoubtedly we all became more conscious of our situation in relation to security and the world situation. That should make us consider our own position very carefully. It is all very well for those opposite to chide me for rising to take part in what is perhaps one of the most important

debates we have had in this house, but our security and our very future depend entirely upon-
The government.
I would hesitate to depend upon the government, in view of the answers that have been given by the Minister of National Defence.
You have depended upon it for the last fourteen years.

Of course you have been there for a long time, but you have outworn your usefulness. So I say the time now has come when we must ask ourselves these questions. Are we properly prepared to defend ourselves? It is all very well for us to gloss over these things; nevertheless the over-all picture becomes very important. The Minister of National Defence has hesitated to make available certain information to the committee. I believe we are adults capable of thinking for ourselves. There is nothing that would arouse a greater national consciousness of our ability to defend ourselves than complete frankness with this House of Commons. If our position were explained it would help to stimulate a regard for our obligations as citizens. I do not think the minister is overburdened with the number of people who are offering to enlist. Advertisements appear in the various journals and appeals are made over the radio. I do not think a frank revelation will bring any comfort to the enemy.
Do not let us fool ourselves. We have only one potential enemy and the Kremlin is already aware of our defence position. I am reminded of the dark days of the war when we were all cautioned against saying anything about the departure of troop ships. It is interesting to note that the shortwave radio in Germany always broadcast the date when a troop ship was leaving. That is only a smoke screen. Let us have the facts. We want to know that the money is being properly spent because it is being advanced by the taxpayers of Canada, not by this government. We want to know the money is fulfilling the purposes for which it was intended.
Some very proper questions have been directed to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton). I presume that in due time he will answer all of them. I was much impressed yesterday afternoon with the remarks of the member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), a man whose background and training fits him not only to ask these questions but to advise any committee the minister may set up to deal with this matter. Mr. Chairman, this is a very grave moment in our 29087-153J
Supply-National Defence history. We have certainly projected ourselves into the future as a power capable of holding our own should the necessity arise. These are the questions that were asked by the member for Nanaimo and I intend to read them into the record. They will be found at page 2397 of Hansard. I am reading these questions to make sure I receive the answers I am seeking.
Order.

Do not interrupt me, please, because as I have already intimated I am only a member of parliament and not a technical adviser. I am much concerned about this matter, however, more concerned than many of the members opposite who are laughing this matter off. I think it is a disgrace to take such an unusual attitude towards one of the most serious matters ever to come before this house. I should like to direct the minister's attention to the questions I mentioned appearing at page 2397 of Hansard.
I ask the minister to explain definitely whether this $19 million is to come out of the amount allocated and voted by this house last year, and whether the $59 million voted at that time will be reduced to this extent. Then I ask him to explain in a little more detail how the division of that money is going to take place, how he proposes to utilize it, under these main headings to which I have referred.
A review of the remarks made by the member for Nanaimo will indicate how important the answers are which we seek. I am sure, Mr. Chairman, if the minister can provide the answers to those questions our concern will be alleviated, especially if he can assure us that his statements in this house bear some relation to the facts. If that is done, there is no doubt about his ability to obtain the sanction he seeks for these estimates. Imagine the talk about bringing comfort to the enemy! May I say to all members that if the answer made by the minister in this house a few days ago, refuted yesterday, followed by the admission of those facts by the minister, has any relation to our over-all defence position, then Canada is an easy mark for any enemy who may care to attack her.
I do not want to be misunderstood, Mr. Chairman, and I say this with the kindliest feelings, but I want to understand what I am voting for when I vote this $19 million.

I should like to ask the minister one or two questions. If a member received an envelope bearing the mark "On His Majesty's Service", and at the bottom the word "Headquarters", would that envelope be from military headquarters?

Evidently it was put in there by one of the officials of that department. Whether it was with the minister's knowledge I do not know. All the members of my party received a copy.

getting the same kind of answer that I received from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) yesterday-nothing.
I protest against that statement. I have been waiting to answer the questions of members opposite for a day and a half. I wish to have an opportunity of doing so.
Mr. Chairman, I sat down so that the minister could reply.
And the member for York South (Mr. Cockeram) caught the chairman's eye before I did.

When discussion took place about the Canadian Commercial Corporation, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) stated that there was within the Department of National Defence a committee from whom requisitions were received by that corporation. I wonder if the minister will give the house the details of that committee, how it functions, and how it goes about obtaining tenders for those large amounts of money.
Then there is another question which perhaps the minister can tell us something about. We are obliged to get most of our information from the minister when he makes speeches outside of the House of Commons. I think the only information we have with regard to the reserve army is that there are approximately 40,000 men in it. The other night the minister told us that there are 40,811 men in the permanent army. We then have a total force, including the reserve army, of 80,000 men. This item includes part of the pay of those men, so I think I am in order in mentioning this matter. But we have a group of civilians, numbering 20,279 as of March 31 this year, servicing that department. In other words, for every man in the permanent force and reserve army there is one man in the civil service servicing the personnel. As I pointed out to the minister the other day, there was an increase of only 108 in the civil service strength in the year; but there was an increase of $12,682,000 in the pay of the civil servants. That works out to in excess of $600 per civil servant working in that department. I point out to the minister that there was surely something wrong with those figures. I should like to make sure that they are correct, because the total increase in pay for the civilian branch of the armed forces for the next fiscal year was $12,682,000, and there is an increase of only 108 in their strength.

A number of questions have been asked and as I indicated a moment ago

I have been waiting for an opportunity to answer them. I should make it perfectly clear at the outset that, so far as I have been able to see from examining the record of the discussions in the house from the start of the session until the beginning of today's sitting, the only two questions which I have not answered were those to which an answer was refused for reasons of security, plus the other two, the answers to which are being prepared by the department and should be available before the house adjourns. I believe I am correct in saying that is the actual fact.
The hon. member for Calgary East during the course of the debate on the address referred to civil defence and I thought that at an appropriate time I should be glad indeed to make a statement on the subject. But as I read his speech at the time and as I have read it this afternoon, I do not see that any questions were asked that have not been answered. If I have not paid him the courtesy of an immediate answer, then I apologize. But I think I am right in the record, that up until today's sitting the only two questions that I have not answered from the beginning of this session were those to which an answer was refused for reasons of security plus the two still standing on the order paper.
In the course of his interesting remarks the hon. member for Nanaimo, as reported at page 2395 of Hansard, said:
The first question I would ask is this:	Is this
amount part of the additional moneys voted for future years? Will there be a reduction from that $59 million, or is this amount to be added on?
In this question he has reference to the commitment authority of some $59 or $60 million for future years. The answer is that the appropriation we are seeking today is in respect of the year 1948-49. The commitment authority of $59 million for future years is in respect of the year 1949-50. Therefore the $19 million is not deducted from the $59 million. One is for cash which we are seeking today to make expenditures which have not been made yet, and the other of course provides for future years commitment authority.
The hon. member also asks:
Can the minister allocate the division he proposes to make of this $19 million under those various main estimates?
I gave a breakdown of that figure before in the course of the discussion, but I read the figures rather rapidly and I shall be glad indeed to give them again. This sum of $19,622,583 is divided as follows: For complete payment in respect of the year 1948-49 to the imperial war graves commission for care and maintenance of graves of the second
Supply-National Defence world war, $127,583; for the navy, due to wage, salary, pay and allowance increases, $1,995,000.
That includes civil servants too, does it?

That is right. For the army there is $14,500,000 of which $5,940,000 is for married quarters which were completed during the year under an accelerated program which we started to build up during the year so as to complete the largest possible number of married quarters during the period. For maintenance of properties, $700,000. For purchase and repair of equipment, $900,000. For increased wages, salaries, pay and allowances, a total of $6,960,000. These figures make up the item of $14,500,000.
The one remaining item is $3 million for the air force. That is for the overhaul of aircraft under a program that was started two years ago and which provided for overhaul and modification this year of 209 aircraft at a cost of over $10 million. It was possible to proceed with that work faster than we had planned, and accordingly more money should be expended on that account than had been provided for in the main estimates. That is the way the items are broken down. The hon. member for Trinity asked for some further information about the North Stars. His question was: "Did the R.C.A.F. need these planes?" The answer is yes. Any air force in a country with the area of Canada, and having to serve not only the length of the country but also to reach well up beyond the Arctic circle, needs high-speed, long-range, load-carrying transport planes. They were asked for by the air force. The hon. member asked whether half of them were ever in service at the same time. I doubt whether it is possible to say that half the aeroplanes of any service are in use at the same time, but service has been normal.
The hon. member referred to the fact that modifications had to be made. Of course that is true. That is true not only of new planes, but also of virtually every old plane. Recently I found that a Rolls-Royce engine, which is one of the most efficient engines there are, and which has been in existence for eight years, is still being modified.
The hon. member also asked whether T.C.A., which at one stage had borrowed six of the planes, had turned them back in a broken down condition. The answer is no. They were completely overhauled and new engines were installed in the planes.
At whose expense?

At the expense of T.C.A. The planes were returned in a condition as good

Supply-National Defence as new, or even better, because in addition some modifications were installed at T.C.A. expense.
Does the minister know how many flying hours each plane had?

No, I cannot give that now but I can easily find it for the hon. member, but I have not got it with me. Then the hon. member referred to the need of a fighter defence force. The hon. member for Grey North took some exception to the fact that I made a comparison with the situation in 1933-34. The hon. member for Trinity made a comparison with Sweden. I would point out that the defence needs of every country must be considered with regard to that country. Recently we have had the pleasure -and it was a very distinct pleasure-and also the advantage of a visit from the chief of the Swedish air staff, General Nordensheld, and we discussed with him the organization and strength of the Swedish air force. He had the opportunity of seeing ours. I am committing no breach of confidence when I say that he referred in terms of the highest commendation to the work he saw going on in our air force. He saw a good deal of it. He recognized, as we do, that the defence needs are quite different for the two countries, and that they have to be met in different ways.
With regard to the question of the air force, and the objections taken to the remark I made in respect of the situation as it existed in 1933-34, I think it has some relevance when people today express their very strong support of the air force, as I think most of us do, to judge how that is likely to be carried out, to consider what happened in the past. It is interesting to note that in 1933-34 the air force was reduced to its lowest strength since the first year of its origin, with a total strength of 692 officers and men regular, and thirty-four in the auxiliary. The defence expenditures for that year were $1,684,561.93, which also included expenses for civil aviation and postal transport. That figure may be contrasted with the amount we are seeking in the main estimates for 1949-50 of $142,836,360.
Does the minister suggest that the situation has not been changed since 1933-34?

I have heard eloquent
speeches from the other side of the house suggesting that at about that time we should have been preparing for the next war, which one hon. member said was coming. From that date on there was a steady improvement.
What about the air training plan?

The air training plan was a grand aerodrome of democracy and produced
131.000	trained air crew, and they arrived when they were needed.
And refused before the war.

The hon. member asked
whether there was any procedure whereby we were cannibalizing Vampires. The answer is no.
What are you cannibalizing?

We are cannibalizing a number of planes, which are virtually obsolete, in order to keep them going without having to start factories working on spare parts; but we are not cannibalizing any modern planes.
Yesterday the minister said that he had 1,000 first-line planes. Does that mean that 1,000 planes are complete and none of them have been cannibalized?

Not at all. Yesterday I said nothing about 1,000 planes. Some hon. member quoted what I said in the house on the estimate debate-I think it was the hon. member for Nanaimo-and gave a partial list of what I gave then.
On Monday.

On Monday I did mention
1.000	planes. We have not got 1,000 first-line planes, and no suggestion has been made that we have.
How many first-line planes have we that are not cannibalized? That is what I should like to know. We are spending practically $150 million on the air force.
I must tell the hon. member that it will require a pretty nice appraisal by people who are experienced in it to say what are first-line and what are not.
The number is sixty-two.

It is a matter of opinion in each case as to what is the most modern type for the purpose for which it is designed. At present we have not sixty-two, as the leader of the opposition said-I assume he means Vampires-but seventy-seven.

I ask the minister to check his figure. He must realize that there have been a number of crashes which reduced the eighty-five below that number, and he also knows that there are a number not yet actually put into service.
We have a number in reserve, but there are seventy-two Vampires either in service, in reserve or undergoing modification at the present time.
The minister said seventy-seven.

I beg your pardon, seventy-seven.
The hon. member for Vancouver South asked me a question about the visit of the Australian defence minister, Sir Frederick Shedden. Sir Frederick Shedden is the permanent secretary of the defence department of Australia. He corresponds to our deputy minister of defence. He is almost the senior civil servant in Australia. He is visiting here and the United States for the purpose of exchanging views on various subjects; but so far as any indication has yet been received here as to the purpose of his visit, it is to discuss organization, administration and matters of that kind. No doubt in addition we shall go on to discuss with him other matters, but the question of a Pacific regional security pact is not on the agenda. May I say a further word or two in reply to what the hon. member for Vancouver South said. The view of the government, of course, is that there is only one possible aggressor at this time, and should that aggressor commit an act of aggression it will affect practically every part of the western and eastern world including Canada. It will be one war in one world.
Is the minister favourable to a Pacific defence pact?

That would be a matter of government policy which I could not deal with now. But I should think a good deal could be said for having regional defence pacts along the lines of the North Atlantic security pact in the hope that they would gradually form part of one defence system which the United Nations was set up to establish, and which we still hope the United Nations will achieve.
The hon. member for Peterborough West asked me about an envelope which he had. That envelope was sent to hon. members enclosing a speech on industrial organization. That speech gave facts and figures which were new, and I thought hon. members would be interested in it. Apparently in addition, by error, he got a pamphlet-
We all got that.
-which he should not have got, certainly, and which I am sure will do him no good whatever.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Does the minister mean the pamphlet is no good whatever?

No; I said I was sure it would do the hon. member for Peterborough West no good whatever.
Supply-National Defence
Why was this pamphlet, The Future of the Liberal Party, by the Hon. Brooke Claxton, distributed at all from the Department of National Defence? That is what I would like to know.
They had nothing to do with paying for it. If the pamphlet was wasted I am sorry; it should have been given to some proper recipient.
But it is taking government money to put it in there.
No.
Who paid the postage?
If anyone suggests that hon. members in any part of the house do not send out political material to their constituents and friends under a government frank, then I am surprised.
That is only one point-
Sit down.
It is not sent out by a separate department.

Now, Mr. Chairman, I believe I have answered the questions which were expressly put to me. If I have not, then no doubt I shall be reminded of it at once. However, I cannot close these remarks without saying a word or two on the more general subjects which have been brought up. This is the first time, I believe, in our experience that anything in the nature of a general debate has occurred on supplementary estimates. I have never heard of a minister being asked to make a general statement on supplementary estimates, and it certainly is not my intention to do so today.
However I should like to offer one or two sentences.
In the first place, with regard to the organization of the armed forces, I believe that we have made, in the field of co-ordination and unification, as great progress as has been made in any other country.
In the second place, in regard to the primary objective of the training of officers, I believe that in our various plans-in the cadet service colleges, in the university training plan, as well as in the command contingent plans we have in the 4,000 officer candidates in training to the equivalent of a university degree, plus a year's practical experience with their service, a greater number, in proportion to our population, training for a high standard than any country in the world.
In the third place, with regard to recruiting for the active force, we have just had the

Supply-National Defence best two months of recruiting since the war. The results for the last six months show an 81 per cent improvement over the corresponding period of the year before. If those numbers are maintained we will continue to obtain the number of men required to build up our armed forces to the strength we believe to be necessary. What is more, the quality is of the kind we need.
Fourth, with regard to the reserve forces, in addition to the 40,000 and more men in the active force, we have 40,000 men in the reserve forces; and when you compare that with the corresponding figure of something like 75,000 in the territorial forces of England, organized on the same basis and for the same purpose, then I suggest we are making good progress. I would like to see many more men in the reserve force. That force as regards equipment and spirit is in much better shape than ever before in peacetime. Then, we have 20,000 civilians doing work which used to be done by service personnel, because it is more economical to do it this way.
Altogether we have had in the department and in the services 100,000 men and women, of whom 60,000 are full-time, who I believe are well qualified to do the jobs they are called upon to do.
Fifth, with regard to equipment, we are 1 believe the first country to undertake the design and construction of a new type of high-speed anti-submarine vessel; three of them will be laid down this year. We are continuing the development of the Orenda engine and the XC-100 night fighter allweather aircraft by A. V. Roe. Tests already made of the engine indicate that in all probability it may be not only a success, but an exceedingly good engine. Our hope is that the plane will be flight tested this summer; and as soon as it is, plans are made for us to go into production on the first jet-engined plane to be designed and entirely built in Canada.
Finally, with regard to relations with the civilian community, the relations between the active and the reserve forces and the relations among the three services, the effort has been made steadily throughout the period since the war to create the idea that this is one partnership essential to the welfare of all of our country. I believe that, commensurate with our resources and commensurate with the program which has been set, they are doing a good job for the defence of Canada.

If it is true that the R.C.A.F. did need 24 North Stars, of which six were lent to T.C.A., then why were another half a dozen or more left in storage?
[Mr. Claxton.l

Those planes were not needed by the R.C.A.F. at the time. They were available for delivery. It was the economical way in which to keep the plant of Canadair operating on an economic scale, so that the planes would have a lower cost than if we ordered only the planes we needed ourselves. At that time it might have been possible for us, for example, to have ordered twelve; and if so the cost would have gone up commensurately, particularly if we had given an order for twelve at first and then eleven more later.
Would the minister tell us something about the defence purchasing board?
Yes; I had overlooked your question.
Then, one other question: Is it not a fact that those planes stored out at Downsview are some of the first North Stars produced, and' that they were reported to be defective.

As to the planes stored at Downsview, I would not think it made any difference which ones were stored there and which were in reserve. As I said yesterday afternoon, our plan is to keep some 25 per cent in reserve for the time being. That number will change. The number will change as there will be a flow backward and forward to meet the needs. I do not think it makes any difference what the order is.

I agree with the minister that it does not make any difference what the order is, but I should like to know whether the planes which are stored and inhibited and all the other things-this can be obtained from the serial numbers-cannibalized-
There is no cannibalizing.
I should like to know whether those planes were among the first delivered to the Royal Canadian Air Force.

I can get the information for the hon. gentleman. In answer to his other question may I say that the procedure whereby the Department of National Defence makes its purchases is that the service concerned, the navy, army or air force, working with the deputy minister and his officials, prepare contract demands. When a contract demand is passed within the department it is sent to the Canadian Commercial Corporation, which advertises for tenders. When the tenders are received they are processed by the Canadian Commercial Corporation and the conclusions are reported to the Department of National

Defence. Observations are expressed and then the tender is awarded.
Consultation is held with the industrial defence board, the Canadian preparedness association and committees of industry with regard to matters of long-term planning but not with regard to individual orders. We have within the Department of National Defence joint service committees on weapons, equipment, clothing and the like so that the services may be in line with regard to various items of equipment.
Will the minister tell us who are on that committee and who are on the imperial defence board? They are the people responsible for spending this money.
No; the people responsible for spending the money are the government of Canada.
They are responsible to you?

No. The industrial defence board and the industrial preparedness association have nothing whatever to do with expenditures of money, with procurement or administration direct. They are consultative bodies, one being appointed by the government and the other being an organization of industry corresponding as far as industrial preparedness is concerned to the Canadian Manufacturers' Association in the field of civilian industry. They have been exceedingly helpful but they have no responsibility. We are very glad to consult them about matters of policy.

There is a committee in the defence department which is responsible for these applications or whatever it is you submit to the Canadian Commercial Corporation. That was stated in the house the other day by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
There must be some misunderstanding about that. We have joint service committees made up of representatives of the three services.
Who are they?

There must be a dozen at various levels. They have no authority whatever for making expenditures. They agree on a common pattern of shoe or a standard of cloth, and then, that having been decided, the order is placed by the service through the deputy minister with the Canadian Commercial Corporation, which corpora-
Supply-National Defence tion makes the purchase, with funds supplied, for the Department of National Defence. There is no committee of the kind described.
Did the Department of National Defence actually requisition or ask the government to approve the purchase of the twenty-four North Stars that the minister says they needed?

I do not want to disclose what I should not, but that was cleared through service levels, and then through the cabinet defence committee. Then a contract demand was formulated in the ordinary way and it came up through the deputy minister and, because of its size, was approved by myself. It was referred to the treasury board, approved by council, and then the order was placed through the Canadian Commercial Corporation with the industry concerned.
The R.C.A.F. actually asked for them, did they?
Yes.

In view of the fact that R.C.A.F. personnel are on twenty-four hour duty at the present time I should like to ask the minister what is being done to improve the housing conditions at the various camps, particularly at Camp Borden, with which I am more familiar. The living quarters for both officers and men are not what they should be at the present time to house men who are on twenty-four hour active service. Some work was contemplated and some work has been done, but I should like to know what is actually being done to improve the living conditions of R.C.A.F. personnel in the various camps.

On January 1, 1947, we had in the armed forces of Canada 1,100 married quarters. That was the total for the navy, army and air force and it included permanent, temporary and emergency quarters. On March 31, 1949, we had either completed or rapidly approaching completion 7,500 married quarters. That was a tremendous increase, a much greater increase, I can assure hon. members than that made in any other country with which comparisons are usually made in such matters. The supplementary estimates which I hope we will pass provide for payments on this accelerated married quarters program of $5,940,000, of which amount $1,630,000 was for additional quarters at Camp Borden.

Supply-Post Office
Are these married quarters being provided under contracts let through Canadian Commercial Corporation or is the work being done by direct day labour under the supervision of the department?

The greatest part of it is being done by contract, but where we could not find a contractor to take the contract or where we wanted to build a special type of quarters it has been done by the Department of National Defence by day labour. For 1949 the greatest part of the married quarters program will be handled by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and we hope that that will provide two years of our married quarters program in one year.

Will the minister look into the matter and do his best to have that service extended?

What was the date of the last increase in the hourly scale of wages paid to printers employed at the government printing bureau?
The answer was, "April 1, 1948." I would point out that these agreements in the city of Montreal and the city of Toronto increasing the wages paid in those cities have come into effect since that date. This is a clear indication of the time lag. Is a further increase under consideration?
I am happy to say that the answer to that question is a categorical "yes". I hope the increase will soon be announced.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Before this item is carried I should like a little information from the Acting Secretary of State about the citizenship branch. This may be one of the smaller branches of the government, but in the minds of many of us it is a very important one. In the last few years many thousands of immigrants have come to Canada. I should like to find out what the government is doing to let those immigrants know something about Canadian citizenship and Canadian culture. I should also like to know what the department has been doing with regard to providing information on citizenship to other Canadians as well.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I would welcome an opportunity to make quite a long speech on this subject, but I do not want to do that at this moment. This is an important branch, one that has become of considerable importance since we enacted the citizenship act and have been bringing many newcomers to this country. The citizenship branch has been in close co-operation with the various provinces. As hon. members know, education is a matter which comes under the jurisdiction of the provinces. The citizenship branch has been in close co-operation with the departments of education in the provinces with the object in view of providing training for the newcomers to Canada.
In addition to that various private organizations have assisted in providing classes, with the result that a large number of classes have been established throughout Canada to give an opportunity to the newcomers to this country to learn the English and the French languages. The item in which I am asking for additional funds today to the amount of $3,779 is to pay half of the cost of some broadcasts which are being made in Ontario. The provincial government is paying the other half. These are broadcasts to explain to the people of the country the problems of the immigrant when he comes to Canada, with the object of securing their co-operation in helping them to become assimilated.
Then we are providing prints of films to be used on board ship, so that when these people are coming to Canada they may learn something of the conditions that they will meet,

Supply-Secretary of State and not be entire strangers when they arrive here. Then the Department of Mines and Resources has published a very good booklet called "This is Canada". We are securing copies of that publication for distribution as we feel it is a pamphlet that can be of great assistance to the teachers who are running classes for the immigrants.
There is a great deal I should like to say on this subject and concerning the Canadian citizenship council, of which General Crerar is the head, which is co-operating by helping to establish classes. The council is in touch with the provinces as well. They really are trying to co-ordinate the activities of the dominion and the provinces with the private organizations such as labour organizations, veterans organizations, and other groups in Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
There are two further questions I should like to ask the minister arising out of what he has said. The minister said that a certain amount of money was being expended on broadcasts in Ontario in conjunction with the provincial government. I should like to know why these broadcasts are not being carried in other provinces as well. If it is a matter of the provincial governments not co-operating, why does not the federal government go ahead on its own and tell the Canadian people something about citizenship problems?
The second question I have in my mind is about the use of films. The minister said that films are being used on ships bringing immigrants over. That is very good. But how far are films being used in this country? We have a vehicle right at our hand, namely, the national film board, which has turned out really splendid work on films dealing with citizenship. Does this particular department use this material in various areas where there are film circuits which are attended by great numbers of people?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The reason that Ontario is the only province in which we are having the joint broadcasts is that it was Ontario which first organized these broadcasts and asked if we would co-operate with them. We agreed to do so. I have no doubt that if other provinces decide to undertake the same sort of educational work, the citizenship branch will be glad to co-operate in a similar way. In regard to films, we are endeavouring to secure films and to make them available to the various classes that are being held, but anything that we produce in that line is after consultation with the departments of education so that we shall not in any way be stepping on the toes of the provincial authorities.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I would not like to get into a jurisdictional dispute with the provinces on education. Surely, in the matter of these broadcasts it is the responsibility of this department to approach the provinces to see if they will co-operate. If not, I do not think any constitutional problem would be involved in using the air waves in these various provinces in giving broadcasts on citizenship. I should like to think that this department of our government was the spearhead of the drive instead of waiting for others to come along and make suggestions to the government.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: This is a new venture. We have tried it out in Ontario, and as the results are ascertained it is quite likely that it will be carried out in other provinces as well.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I should like to follow what the hon. member for Winnipeg North has said and suggest that the C.B.C. be used, as it is now being used to give some excellent programs on science, medicine and other subjects which are of wide general interest. It might well be used to take the place of some of the brain-softening soap programs that are on the air in the morning. It would not hurt our own Canadian women to have little citizenship talks as well. If we could have some really good general programs explaining the growth of democratic institutions and the practices that we use to make democracy work it would be all to the good. There is nothing in the world to prevent the C.B.C. from doing for citizenship what it is now doing in these programs for science.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The C.B.C. has been putting out some very good programs dealing with the problems of immigrants to help them become assimilated when they reach the various parts of Canada.
