638. To reimburse the Canadian Commercial Corporation for amounts advanced by it as working capital under mortgage security to George T. Davie and Sons Limited (losses on which advances cannot yet be estimated) for the purpose of enabling that company to complete and to deliver ships to the Ming Sung Industrial Company Limited, which purchased such ships with funds derived mainly from a loan for this purpose guaranteed by Canada under part II of the Export Credits Insurance Act, $850,000.

Perhaps I had better explain this situation. At the outset I may say it is one that has given the Department of Trade and Commerce a great deal of worry over a long period. The transactions undertaken by the government, which in the result have made necessary this special vote, were carried on under the authority of part II of the Export Credits Insurance Act, 1944. It will be remembered that this act was introduced as part of this government's program in the immediate post-war period, looking to the rehabilitation of the war-torn countries and the maintenance of our export trade. The act was divided into two separate parts, of which the first provided the authority under which the Export Credits Insurance Corporation was established. Part II of the act was the enabling legislation for the extension of government to government credits, as distinct from the credit insurance facilities available to private exporters through the corporation.
Supply-Trade and Commerce
We are not here concerned with the corporations. Part II of the act, the part dealing with government to government credits, made provision for two distinct types of credit facilities. The more important of these was for direct government to government loans, which were authorized to an aggregate of $750 million, of which amounts totaling $594,500,000 were advanced. Full details of these loans have been laid before parliament from time to time by my colleague the Minister of Finance.
The second type of credit facility that was made available under part II of the act was provided by subparagraph (a) of paragraph (1) of section 22. Under this section the governor in council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce, was permitted to authorize the Minister of Finance to guarantee the obligations of the government or any agency of the government of any such other country to pay the cost of Canadian-produced goods under a contract to purchase such goods from an exporter.
Only two guarantees under the provisions of this particular subsection were made, one of which was subsequently converted into a direct government to government advance. The other guarantee was the transaction with which we are here concerned. Under this transaction the Minister of Finance gave guarantees to a group of Canadian banks in respect of credits provided by them to the Ming Sung Industrial Company Limited, a Chinese corporation borrowing under the authority of and with the guarantee of the Chinese government. These loans were to enable the company to purchase specially designed ships and other equipment in Canada for use in its shipping operations on the Yangtze river. In accordance with the provisions of the act the Chinese government, having guaranteed the obligations of the Ming Sung Industrial Company Limited, requested the Canadian government to do so as well, indemnifying the Canadian government against loss in connection therewith. Total credits made available by the banks were to finance not more than 85 per cent of the program of purchases in Canada of ships and related equipment and services by the Ming Sung Industrial Company Limited, and were limited to a maximum of $12,750,000. That is the part that guaranteed the actual transaction; provisions were made for an expenditure of $15 million. Under the terms of the agreement the company was to provide $2,250,000 in cash, making a total purchasing program of $15 million.
The major part of this program consisted of the following three shipbuilding contracts: one contract with St. Lawrence Metal and

Supply-Trade and Commerce Marine Works Incorporated covering four 160-foot L.B.P. Yangtze freight and passenger vessels, and two contracts with George T. Davie and Sons Limited covering two 160-foot vessels and three 270-foot Yangtze freight and passenger vessels. These contracts were negotiated on a firm price basis, with provision for the making of change orders from time to time as might be considered necessary by the purchaser.
Within a few weeks of the signing of the contracts the owner and manager of the Davie yard, Mr. Charles Davie, was killed in a motorcar accident, leaving that yard without experienced management. Construction under these contracts was carried on, but by August, 1948, before any of the ships had been delivered, it was apparent that owing to increases in the cost of materials and labour and as a result of disputes between the builders and the purchaser on the interpretation of specifications and extra charges in respect of change orders, neither yard was prepared nor indeed financially able to fulfil its obligations to make delivery in accordance with the terms of the contract. The yards asked that the original contracts be renegotiated. The Ming Sung company on the other hand demanded its rights to delivery in accordance with the terms of the contracts, refused to renegotiate and claimed inability to increase its over-all $15 million program due to Chinese foreign exchange regulations.
When was the original contract made?

I think it was about 1946. Numerous conferences were held between the builders and the purchaser, but it was found impossible to reach an agreement. The purchaser threatened legal action to obtain possession of the ships, relying on a provision in the contracts which gave them the right to enter the yards and complete construction. The yards, on the other hand, threatened a countersuit for extra costs which they claimed were due to them but which the purchaser refused to recognize.
At this point the purchaser and both the yards approached the government in the hope of working out some compromise that would avoid protracted litigation, the probable bankruptcy of both yards and the probability if not the certainty of very substantial losses to the government under its guarantee obligations. Then followed a series of negotiations between the yards, the purchasers and the government. The government's position may be summarized as follows. It had sponsored, by its guarantee, a transaction which in the circumstances threatened to result in the very opposite of the purposes for which the whole post-war program of assist-


ance to war-torn countries had been undertaken-a black eye in the shipping world for the reputation of Canadian shipyards and indeed of Canadian exporters generally; ill will on the part of a country that Canada sought to assist; the certain bankruptcy of two Canadian shipyards; and the very real possibility that the purchaser might, in the face of protracted delays, abandon his interest in the contracts, leaving the government to dispose of specially designed ships which would have little realizable value.
Investigation of the accounts of the yards disclosed aggregate expenditures and firm commitments made by the yards of $10,743,000, and an estimated cost to complete the contracts of $2,703,000, being $2,300,000 in excess of the original contract prices plus agreed extras. It was apparent that the settlement of these excess costs would in equity call for some share to be borne by each of the three parties concerned, the yards, the purchasers and the government. After much negotiation it was agreed as between the government and the Ming Sung company that the company would cancel all items in its original $15 million program for which firm commitments had not been made, being purchases of special equipment, spare parts, et cetera, and would thereby be enabled to pay the resultant savings, amounting to $734,000, in addition to the contract prices and agreed extras. It will be seen that this represented just under one-third of the total extra costs in dispute. The amount of $734,000 was made up of $75,000 in respect of each of the six smaller ships and approximately $94,000 in respect of each of the three larger ships. In consideration of these payments, the government undertook to guarantee delivery of the ships. The St. Lawrence Metal and Marine Works Incorporated accepted settlement on this basis, that is, on payment of an extra $300,000 being $75,000 for each of the four 160-foot ships that it was building, and absorbed the balance of the extra costs that it incurred over the contract prices. It thereupon made delivery to the satisfaction of the purchaser at no cost to the crown.
The George T. Davie Company, however, which had the other contract and which was not so far advanced in construction, advised the government, and substantiated its claim, that it could not complete its contracts without financial assistance. The government, recognizing a measure of responsibility, then undertook to make advances to the Davie company to enable completion of the ships, taking in exchange a first mortgage on the Davie yard. It was recognized that a substantial part of these advances would ultimately have to be written off, but until the

final cost of the ships was determined and the actual loss on the contracts established, a final settlement with the yard could not be made.
To carry out the settlement, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) instructed the Canadian Commercial Corporation to take such action as was necessary to give effect to the foregoing arrangement, and to expedite construction of the vessels under the Davie contracts. The corporation has since that date maintained close technical and financial supervision over the operations of the Davie yard, with the result that delivery has been made of two 160-foot freighters, and two of the three 270-foot vessels. It is expected that the third and last of the large vessels will be completed by June of this year.
On the basis of advances which have been made to date by the Canadian Commercial Corporation to meet the cash deficiencies on operations, and upon statements of estimated cost to completion of the final vessel, the total net advances by the corporation will amount to about $850,000. When the contracts have been completed, the net amount of the government advances determined, and the final costs established by a treasury cost audit, the government will have to write off a substantial part of its advances and make a settlement with the yard which will have regard to the yard's then financial position and future prospects. It is the government's hope that the settlement may be such as to enable the yard to continue as a going concern, the government receiving partial repayment of its advances over a period.
I may say that, before that course was taken, the government's position under every alternative settlement was studied. I am a great believer in taking my losses quickly and avoiding litigation. Had the government not taken that position, there is no doubt the two yards would have gone into bankruptcy and the settlement would have been worked out from that point. I take the full responsibility for the transaction. It was made on my recommendation. I am satisfied today that it was the wisest procedure from the viewpoint of the federal treasury to extricate these yards from the position they were in [DOT]at the time.

It
seems to me that there are two questions that arise. First of all, I am going to ask the minister to explain what authority there was for the Canadian Commercial Corporation coming into this picture. I cannot find any authority in the statutes for it.
Before we come to that, however, I wish the minister would explain just a little
Supply-Trade and Commerce further why it was, in the year 1946, when he said these contracts were entered into, when employment was high and so on, the government felt it necessary to risk public money to that extent. Was it for the purpose of maintaining shipbuilding? If so, were these two yards in a special position? Were they without work? Will the minister make clear why it was necessary to go into it? I am inclined to agree with the minister that when you get into a mess of that kind there is a great deal to be said for cutting your losses and getting out of it. The thing that is not clear to me is just why we got into it and, secondly, how any justification was found for using the Canadian Commercial Corporation to fill the breach.
Mr. Chairman, the transactions were entered into in pursuance of legislation passed by this parliament.
That is the Export Credits Insurance Act?
Yes; they are all made under that act.
That seems perfectly clear.

There were two types of transactions made possible by that act. One was government to government loans and the second was contractual arrangements between private parties in each country. A reliable firm of merchants in China, we will say, could make arrangements with shipyards in Canada. This transaction must have the guarantee of the government of China and the government of Canada. This was a transaction of that type. It seemed to me at the time that this was a more desirable transaction than a direct government to government loan.
A private loan with the backing of the government, had the assurance of a contract between a reliable merchant in one country and a private firm in this country, making use of the banking system of both countries as the intermediary. In addition, it had the government guarantee, which is just as good an endorsement, on paper, as is a direct government obligation. I have no reason today to believe that this is not a desirable transaction. The Ming Sung Company is one of the oldest shipping companies in China. The company has enjoyed a favourable reputation for several hundred years, and there is every indication that its obligations will be met when due.
The difficulty was that the situation developed as it did. The possibilities of obtaining further guarantees in China were doubtful. The government was tottering at that time.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The Chinese government?

The Chinese government. In any event, it was felt it would not be desirable to increase the obligations beyond $15 million, which had been arranged. It was arranged that the loss should be shared three ways. The Ming Sung Company cancelled certain contracts it had placed for spare parts and thus raised approximately another $800,000. The audited claims of the shipbuilders were reduced by $800,000, so that two shipyards took a one-third loss and the government took the residual third. The government took a possible loss of $850,000 and for that it has as security a mortgage on one of the shipbuilding yards.

I
understand that part; but I am still not clear as to why in 1946 the government felt it was necessary to step into this situation. Was it because they felt it necessary to provide business for Canadian shipbuilding yards? Why could they not allow ordinary business operations to take care of themselves? As I say, it was a time of high employment. The minister still has not made clear to me what it was that moved the government. Was it a desire to serve China? Was it a desire to serve our own shipbuilding companies, or what?
It is all very well now to say that it was a time of high employment. Those who occupied the opposite benches at that time told us we would be in the depths of a depression in 1946.

But
you were telling us it was a period of high employment, and it has been.

The contracts now before us were made as one of a number of arrangements to try to tide us over a situation which many people believed would be very difficult, the period of demobilization when the men were returning from the war. I say the contract was made in 1946 and I think it was. But I imagine the negotiations were entered into in 1945. At the same time, we negotiated government to government contracts for a number of other ships.

Will the minister deal with the other question? I understand fully how the original contract was entered into under the Export Credits Insurance Act, part II. I do not understand where you find any power in' the Canadian Commercial Corporation Act for bringing that corporation into this situation. It seems to me that this situation should have been disclosed and the government should have

obtained some fresh authority to deal with it. I can discover no authority for the Canadian Commercial Corporation to deal with it, and that is what I want to know. As it stands now, it seems to me you have acted without any authority whatever. Will you explain that?

Parliament was not sitting when this problem developed. It is sitting now. As soon as parliament resumes we get our authority. We stepped into the breach to protect a government credit of $12 million and to avoid an ugly situation which might well have meant the loss of that amount. It could easily have done so. We stepped into the breach. We did it with the authority of the governor in council, which is the only authority we can get between parliaments for emergency action of that kind. As far as the Canadian Commercial Corporation is concerned, there is authority under the act to carry out the instructions of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The corporation acts as the agent of the Minister of Trade and Commerce in buying for the armed services.
Yes, for the armed services.
It also acts as agent of the Minister of Trade and Commerce for making purchases on behalf of the Department of Trade and Commerce.

The
minister says quite truly that they act as the agent of the Department of National Defence for making purchases for that department. But there is no suggestion that this had anything to do with the Department of National Defence. The minister really must get down to the business of pointing out to us where there is some authority.
It had something to do with the Department of Trade and Commerce, had it not?

You
cannot use the money of the Canadian Commercial Corporation except for certain specific purposes which are set out here. Did the minister or the department not consider its legal position with the Department of Justice?
Certainly.
What advice did you get from the Department of Justice?
Is my hon. friend setting up the thesis that, if a sudden emergency occurs between sessions of parliament, nothing can be done?

I am
not setting that up at all. But I am setting up that what has been done seems to have had

no legal justification whatever. I am not saying whether there was some way in which it could have been dealt with or not. I should think possibly there was. But I cannot see that this was the way. I think the minister should take the trouble, if the legal position was considered, to let us know what was said; because as it stands now it seems to me that this is just another of those things really worse than the ordinary order in council. The ordinary order in council does usually have something to back it up. But here the minister has as yet shown no authority of any kind, so far as I can see. Surely we cannot leave it at that.

The procedure was worked out by the officers of the Department of Trade and Commerce and the officers of the Department of Finance. The procedure was agreed between the two departments as the logical one in the circumstances. The approval of council was obtained. I think if my hon. friend will look at the files of this parliament he will find that the order in council has been on file for a considerable period. I shall be glad to get him another copy. I cannot think what more authority we can get.
Carried.

No,
Mr. Chairman, it is not carried. The minister has not yet answered my question. He just says that they were faced with a difficulty, that they decided they had better deal with it, and the departments got together. I thought he said a moment ago that they had sought the advice of the justice department, but apparently that was not done. I do not think this item should go through yet. I think there should be a further explanation. A further explanation must be given. If they did consult the justice department, we should know the advice that was given. If they did not consult the justice department, it is clear that they should have, and that they have just gone ahead regardless of any authority. I think this item should stand.

I may say here that there is an officer of the Department of Justice attached to the Department of Trade and Commerce and there is also an officer of the Department of Justice attached to the Department of Finance. We had the judgment of those two officers. I do not say we had written opinions. I do not see anything on which we should get an opinion. But in any case we had the advice of the Department of Justice.

The
minister says he does not see that there is anything he should get an opinion on. Nevertheless he is faced with the fact that there is not, as far as I can discover, and he has
Supply-Trade and Commerce not shown it to me, a shadow of justification for what has been done. If the law officers or the legal officers in the department were consulted, it is strange to me if there was no written memorandum of any kind. I suggest there may be something further, and I think this item should stand. I do not want to waste the time of the committee but it seems to me to be a very high-handed procedure. We have no desire to drag this committee's work out any more than anyone else but it is clear to me, as far as I can see, that it was a perfectly high-handed action and that we should not acquiesce in it. I think possibly the minister may be able to make out a better case than he has done up to the present time. But as far as I can see, he has made out no case.

I think this department is in the same position as any other. We are coming to parliament and asking it to approve or disapprove. If parliament disapproves, the government is defeated. If parliament approves, the item will be confirmed by parliament. But it will not be permitted to stand. It will be dealt with now.

This is the result of a government guarantee. I have seen statements of this Canadian export company for some years. What surprises me is the low rate they have charged private exporters for their guarantee. As I recall it, the amount was infinitesimal- 002 or something like that. The result is that the Canadian export credit company have no surplus at all. Practically all the money they got in was from interest on bonds which they had purchased from the government. This is a large amount. I should like to know from the minister what rate they charged exporters to guarantee private people's exports.
I think my hon. friend is referring to the insurance corporation, is he not?
Yes.

That is not the matter that we are discussing. The corporation was formed under the act to which he refers, but there were two parts to the act. There was one part which authorizes transactions of the insurance corporation, and the second part which authorizes direct government to government loans-and I might say that some $600 million was loaned under that provision, government to government-and also includes provision for contracts between private firms with the guarantee of both governments. It was under that third provision that this action was taken.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
To reply to my friend the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, I might say that the assistant deputy minister of justice is a director of the Canadian Commercial Corporation, and it was his opinion that the action taken by the corporation was legal and proper for the corporation.

In
writing?
Well, I have that advice from my deputy minister. It must have been in writing, I should think.
Will the minister give us some information about the experience of the shipbuilding firms? Were they operating as shipbuilding firms during the war?
Yes.
Did they have contracts from the government during the war for building ships?
Yes. Charles T. Davie was one of our most efficient builders of corvettes and frigates.
Charles Davie?

George T. Davie yard. I am mixed up with the owner whose name was Charles Davie. It is the George T. Davie yard. There are two shipyards at Levis, one owned by the Canada Steamship Lines and the other owned by the Davie family. This is the latter. It was an efficient yard, and like all shipyards it was greatly expanded during the war. The St. Lawrence Metal and Marine yard also built a considerable number of corvettes. It is located in the city of Quebec. It was an extremely active shipyard during the war period.
Do I understand also that this sum of money that you found it necessary to advance was in 1946?
No. It is within the last six months.
Within the last six months?

Yes. The advance is guaranteed by a mortgage on the company property. The difficulty came when the first deliveries were about to be made. It was found that large sums of money were owing by Davie and by St. Lawrence Metal and Marine. It was found that without intervention from somewhere it was impossible to deliver the boats, because mechanics' liens would have been filed immediately had delivery been attempted at that stage.

What surprises me, Mr. Chairman, is that experienced shipping com-

panies of this particular kind, which did nol suffer any particular period of bad business during the earlier years, should almosl immediately on the conclusion of the war find themselves in such difficulties that they could not carry out these contracts and the government had to come to their aid. It is easy enough to run any business in that way if one can just carry on and fall flat upon the government to get it out of the hole. The fact that the government did something of this particular nature is more amazing, if it did it without authority, though I understand the minister to say that he did have an order in council for this.
Certainly.

Which presumably is his authority. However, it is more surprising still to find out that this much-vaunted private enterprise found itself in such a hole that the government had to come to its rescue to the tune of $850,000.

Unfortunately private enterprise has to be somewhat venturesome. These people ventured in 1946 and took a firm price contract to deliver nine ships. My hon. friend will recognize that the cost of material and labour advanced materially between 1946 and 1948 when the ships were due to be delivered. One of them is not delivered yet.
If we had had price control we would not have had that trouble.
Perhaps that is why we are paying $850,000.
I was interested in the minister's statement in which he said that the loss was according to the accounting firms of the shipping companies.
No, I did not say that.
I should like to know what effort was made by the government to ascertain whether or not the statement of the company as to its losses was correct.

The first thing the government did was to call in a firm of chartered accountants to go through the records of the company from the beginning. The firm of McDonald Currie Company was retained, and no action was taken by the government until a complete report was obtained.
What is the security of this company behind the mortgage that the government now has?
A first mortgage on the company's real property. What it is worth I cannot say.

Has the minister any
approximate figure?
No, I have no idea.

It
seems strange that the minister and I have to delve into these legal matters. Apparently the government finds itself in the position where this business transaction has to be carried out. It is not a matter whether they have power or not, they just do it. The minister seems to think that by passing an order in council they can cure any difficulty in their position. I propose to read the enabling sections of the act because I believe that if hon. members will listen to it they will find out that this transaction does not appear to come anywhere near to being covered. I am reading from section 4 of the Canadian Commercial Corporation Act:
The corporation is established for the following purposes:-
(a)	to assist in the development of trade between Canada and other nations, and
(b)	to assist persons in Canada
(i)	to obtain goods and commodities from outside Canada; and
(ii)	to dispose of goods and commodities that are available for export from Canada.
I do not think anyone will suggest that what I have read covers what has been done. Section 5 under "powers" makes the situation still clearer. It reads:
(1) The corporation may do such things as it deems expedient for, or conducive to, the attainment of the purposes set forth in section four of this act; and, for greater certainty, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing, the corporation may carry on the business of:-
(a)	importing goods or commodities into Canada, and
(b)	exporting goods or commodities from Canada, either as principal or as agent, in such manner and to such extent as it deems advisable to achieve the said purposes.
In the following year the powers of the corporation were broadened. By chapter 51 of 1947 they were given quite a broad additional power, which reads as follows:
17. The corporation may, as directed by the minister, exercise and perform on behalf of the minister, the power, duty and function vested in the minister to buy or otherwise acquire and manufacture or otherwise produce munitions of war or supplies for, and to construct or carry out projects required by, the Department of National Defence.
In other words, this section gives them certain powers to act as agent of the Department of National Defence. Previously they had certain powers with regard to assisting in the import of goods into, and the export of goods from, Canada. Does the minister suggest that what has been done comes within any of these sections? If not, where is the power? Surely the minister is not going to leave us with the suggestion that merely because the government thinks it wise to do something, they proceed to do it regardless of whether this parliament has given them
Supply-Trade and Commerce power or not. That is the position in which he has left us at the moment.

I should be very glad to enter into a legal argument. I think that if this corporation has the power to deal with the building of ships, which it certainly has, because it has done just that, and to deal with ships for the account of foreign purchasers, it has the power to intervene in a contract of that kind. However, I took the opinion of the assistant deputy minister of justice who was acting in his capacity as-

Let us
see the opinion.

Well, I do not know that I have to do that. He is a director of the Canadian Commercial Corporation, and he gave it as his opinion that the transaction was within the powers of the corporation. My own departmental solicitor, who is an officer of the Department of Justice, gave the opinion that the transaction was in order from the legal point of view. I relied on those two opinions. If my hon. friend has another opinion I shall consider the fact that he has not practised law very much either.

I am
not setting myself up as a lawyer. It does not need a lawyer. It needs only a little common sense to read these things and to see that prima facie they do not cover what has to be done. The minister has become a lot surer about these legal opinions in the last half hour.
Yes, I just obtained that advice from my deputy.

When we first began the discussion I could not make out whether he had any opinion or not. I still think we are entitled to know. Whatever the minister may think about me, there are on this side some hon. members who are quite competent lawyers and I think we are entitled to see the opinion, if one is in writing. If not, maybe we should hear the views of the deputy minister of justice. We would respect his opinion, if that is his opinion. But as it is at present, we are just being treated as we have sometimes been treated before, as people who really need not be answered. The government goes ahead, and it becomes so accustomed to using these powers that it simply does so.

May I ask the minister a question. I am not going to dispute the legality or otherwise of it. The minister may have given this answer in his statement, which was quite lengthy, and I may have missed it. If so, I should like him to give it again a little more simply and precisely.

Supply-Trade and Commerce Apparently the government came to the rescue of a concern that was in financial difficulties. According to the dominion bureau of statistics, commercial failures have been fairly extensive in the last few years. It is obvious that the government has no intention of coming to the rescue of other commercial enterprises which show indications of failure. What was the peculiar circumstance that brought the government to the rescue in this case, and in what other cases would the government likely come to the rescue of prospective commercial failures?

I point out to my hon. friend that the government came to the rescue of itself. The government had guaranteed a $12 million loan to pay for these ships. They did not rescue one shipyard, because after the ships were launched the St. Lawrence Metal and Marine went into receivership. It is in receivership now. The George T. Davie Company turned over to the government all of its physical assets. I do not know that it could have done any more, and its future is pretty well in the hands of the government. It was not to rescue anyone except itself that the government entered into this situation. But if it had not entered in, the ships would not have been delivered. The guarantee of the Chinese government, without ships, would not have been very valuable; and the chances of realizing very much from the sale of the ships which were built to Chinese specifications for a particular trade on the Yangtze river would not have been sufficient to recoup the government to any great extent. I would like to make it clear, though, that the government was helping itself, and no one else.

I can understand anyone doing anything to help himself. That is common sense. Then, may I ask if the guarantee of the Chinese government is still good, because the government at that time seemed to be more stable than the government of today.

All I wish to say is that the government of China paid its obligations at the beginning of this year in full, and cfn time. I have considerable confidence that the government of China will continue to do that. It is only an opinion, but I think there is a good deal of evidence to support it.

The minister has told us that the deputy minister of justice is of the opinion, or that he has the opinion of the deputy minister, that this action is within the purview of the statute.
I suggest that the Minister of Justice will not agree with that, and I doubt very much if the deputy minister of justice ever gave such an opinion. Therefore I would like to see the opinion. I have the greatest respect in the world for Mr. Varcoe's opinion, but I do not 
think he ever gave any opinion, as expressed to the committee now by the minister as having come from the deputy minister of justice. The mere fact that he is a director is not important; he is a director of many things, and does not even attend meetings, because he has too many things to do.
I should like to know who it was that, as a lawyer, gave the opinion that this expenditure was within the power of the government under the statute creating the corporation.

I do not know that I can say anything more than I have already said. There was the departmental solicitor of the Department of Trade and Commerce, Mr. Anger, who was an officer of the Department of Justice; and there was the representative of the Department of Justice on the board of the Canadian Commercial Corporation who, I believe, is Mr. Varcoe, the deputy minister himself.
Should not this have been charged up to the Export Credits Corporation in the first instance?
No, it was a private banking transaction. The loans were actually made by three Canadian chartered banks.

Are there many other
accounts guaranteed by this corporation which are likely to arrive at the same condition?
No, this happens to be the only one.

Mr. Chairman, let us deal with this in an atmosphere of practical common sense. The act, here, is perfectly clear as to the purposes for which this corporation was created. Those purposes are contained in section 4, with a later amendment in the following year providing that this corporation shall have authority to act as purchasing agent on behalf of the Department of National Defence. It has been pointed out-and I am satisfied it is pointed out with accuracy-that the transaction covered by this item does not come within the scope of section 4.
Would my hon. friend read section 4 (b) Cii)?

It reads:
To dispose of goods and commodities that are available for export from Canada.

Yes, and as follows:
The corporation shall comply with any genera] or special direction given by the governor in council or the minister with reference to carrying out its purposes.

Yes-"with reference to carrying out its purposes." But it must be shown that what is being done is within the purposes set out in section 4. It has been contended that they do not come within section 4, and there

is no suggestion of any explanation which would indicate that they do come within that section.
It is not sufficient for a minister of the crown to get up and say, "We think this was a good thing to do." It may be good, or it may be bad. But the first requirement, in dealing with a matter of this sort, is that an explanation be given to the house as to the statutory provision under which the order in council was passed. That is what is being asked now.
It is known to every member of the committee that, if there is a written opinion of Mr. Varcoe, if the Minister of Trade and Commerce would send a message to his department that opinion could be brought back here in ten minutes. I do not believe members of the committee should pass this item until the minister is prepared to produce that opinion which, he says, is on file and can be produced in ten minutes, while we are dealing with other matters.
I did not say that. Will my hon. friend concede this, that after this item is passed by this parliament it will be in order in any event.

No, I am not prepared to concede that. And I am glad the minister raised that point, because already we have come to that very idea. You put something forward in the estimates; you pass the estimates, and then have power of a statutory enactment of the House of Commons. Members of the house have a duty to know on what basis they are dealing with estimates when subsequently they acquire statutory power. The Auditor General has pointed out already in his very last report the tendency of this government to deal with matters without examining what the statutory power is. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is well aware that in the last report of the Auditor General there are several reports of transactions of this very kind, carried out with the statutory authority of an order in council, and without adequate coverage by the act itself.
Surely, if there is an opinion of the deputy minister of justice to the effect that this procedure is within the act, the House of Commons is entitled to have that opinion. If it is not yet in written form it could be put in written form in a short time. But surely in a matter of this kind, with a transaction dealing with a guarantee under a mortgage, there must have been some written record, and it should be before us.

642. Incentive bonus to industry to expedite the production of strategic building materials-further amount required, $135,000.

From time to time the Minister of Trade and Commerce has announced in the house incentive bonuses to various industries for various purposes in connection with the urgent needs of Canadian consumers. My understanding of most of these incentive bonuses is that there has been a payment on the part of the government to certain industries, and that that has been the end of the matter. No guarantee is forthcoming from the industry as to what will be the quid pro quo so far as the Canadian consumer is concerned. I am willing to stand corrected if my understanding is wrong.	What industries
are concerned in this sum of $135,000 asked in addition to the amount passed last session? What amount goes to each of the industries, and what is the quid pro quo to be received for guaranteeing these sums?

We were anxious to obtain additional toilet equipment and also additional foundry products. Both were vitally needed in the house-building program. In order to obtain increased production it was necessary to expand the plant. We wished to have no part in the cost of expansion, but we did offer a bonus of two cents per pound for additional production over a period which ended December 31, 1948. It was estimated that the Port Hope Sanitary Manufacturing Company Limited would produce 8,500,000 pounds; they actually produced 8,100,000 pounds and received a bonus of $162,000, which was inside the estimate. The production of the Anthes-Imperial Company was approximately 17,000,000 pounds, with the bonus amounting to $340,000. The original estimate was for only 10,400,000 pounds or $208,000, which meant that there was a balance payable of $132,000 under the terms of the contract.

Was this solely for bathtubs?
2438	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce
No, for soil pipe and foundry-products for housing.
Was the bonus made available to any company that wished to apply for it?
Yes, any company in the business.
It will be concluded with this payment?
It is all wound up.
There was quite a large vote for Crane Limited?
That is the Port Hope Sanitary.

I discussed this matter in the house some years back at a time when $10,000 houses were being offered for sale with extra plumbing equipment. When a subsidy of this sort is provided, does the government endeavour to find out whether the plumbing supplies are being made available for rural and low-cost housing or whether they are going into luxury hotels and housing?
The plumbing fixtures were Touted into priority housing, which my hon. friend knows is low-cost housing.

Was there any way of knowing whether Crane Limited, which got a subsidy of $400,000, were using that subsidy in order to make material available for the type of house that was advertised as having an extra bathroom? It seems to me that the man who is installing two bathrooms in a 'house should not receive the benefit of a subsidy from the government. If the subsidy was being used to make plumbing material available for rural housing, where there was no plumbing, or for low-cost housing, with a view to getting the cost down, then I think there would be some justification; but I do not think we should be asked to vote a subsidy or a bonus to be used to provide additional bathroom facilities where one bathroom would do.

There is no doubt that a considerable expansion was necessary both in the toiletware field and in the soil-pipe field. My hon. friend knows that those were the two great bottlenecks in housing two or three years ago. Today there is an ample supply of both owing to the fact that plant facilities have been extended, and as a consequence of this subsidy to which I have made reference.
The minister has given a complete list of the firms that have received subsidies under this grant?

Just the two firms.
I Mr. Probe.]
Is the subsidy exhausted or are there any contracts outstanding for the payment of subsidies that would create a contingent liability?
No, the subsidies were terminated on December 31, 1948.
Is it contemplated that the department will be looking for further opportunities to enter into such contracts for the expansion of production of building materials?
No, the house building supply field is fairly well in balance and seems to be taken care of.

Can the
minister give us an estimate of the capital cost involved in the expansion undertaken?
I could not say, except that I do know that it was considerably in excess of the amount received by way of subsidy.
Item agreed to.
643. Departmental administration-further amount required, $25,000.

I understand that earlier this week the House of Commons in the United Kingdom approved the international convention on safety of life at sea and I was wondering if the Minister of Transport could explain to the house Canada's position with regard to that convention. This press article indicates that so far the United Kingdom is the only country that has approved the convention.

I do not know that I can tell the hon. gentleman a great deal at this stage. The convention has not been submitted to the house although it has been tabled. There are one or two methods that could be followed in order to have it ratified. One method would be amendments to the Canada Shipping Act and another would be to place on the order paper a resolution recommending the adoption of the convention. If Canada decides to implement the convention there will be an item in the estimates in order that this matter may be fully discussed.
Has Canada actually signed the convention?
The convention has been signed by the delegation, yes, subject to ratification.
How long ago?

I would think, ten months
ago. I tabled the convention approximately a week after the opening of the session.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The item before the committee has to do with telephones, telegrams, postage, printing, stationery and so on, and the discussion should be confined to those things.

With all due deference, I submit that that is a new ruling. We are dealing with the administration item and on all other such items in these supplementary estimates the discussion has not been confined to the actual articles which were to be paid for. I submit that to make a ruling of that kind now would mean that the same thing would apply to the general estimates, which would mean a complete breaking down of the practice which has been followed in dealing with estimates.
The matter I am raising is of great importance on the west coast. Representations are being made to us, as the minister knows, as to whether or not there should be radio operators on the ships. A practice has been followed by some shipping companies of using what they call a combined operator which means that the particular person will have more than one job. At one time he will be looking after the wireless and at another time he will be checking freight or doing some other job about the ship.
There would seem to be considerable danger that a shipwreck will occur because of these radio operators being asked to do more than look after the radio equipment and signals. I understand that radio telephones are being used a great deal and the suggestion is being made that they should replace the wireless. One difficulty with the radio telephone is that in case of accident it cannot be used to communicate with a ship which may be close by. This whole situation is causing uncertainty which may result in the loss of life. I hope the situation is not that serious, but I believe that possibility exists. If this convention is approved by Canada I understand that difficulty will be met, and that then we will have regulations calling for a wireless operator to be on duty. So the whole question is very important. The minister has said that if we approved the convention we probably would require amendments to the Canada Shipping Act. I would hope that whatever steps are to be taken could be taken without further delay, because of the fact that the possibility of loss of life is involved.

I have received, as have the departmental officials, representations concerning the point brought up by the hon. member; but in order to meet that point, which of course is important, the Canada Shipping Act would have to be amended, as
Supply-Transport
I said a moment ago, either by implementing all the recommendations of the safety of life at sea convention or by bringing down a resolution to that effect. One of the terms of the safety of life at sea convention stipulates that a country ratifying the convention need not do so before 1951. It is a voluminous document, as my hon. friend knows, and the officers of my department feel that before they deal with it substantially they should give it careful consideration. It is not the intention, at this time at least, to amend the Canada Shipping Act; but I believe the officers have in mind the point raised by the hon. member and will do whatever can be done without bringing into effect for the time being the recommendations of the convention.
How can that situation be met without an amendment of the Canada Shipping Act?
I do not know of any way it could be done without amending the act, but the officers of my department are looking into the position to ascertain what can be done.

We also have complaints of infractions of the Canada Shipping Act as it stands at present; that some of the shipping companies are not living up to the act and nothing is being done about it. I wonder if the minister would see that his department makes a check in regard to these complaints. It may be that some of the danger could be avoided by having a closer check on the operation of the ships at the present time and under the present act.
I shall be glad to have that done.

The minister will remember that last year a statute was passed which lifted from the Canada Shipping Act some seventy-odd sections, many of which had to do with the safety of crew and passengers. I am referring in particular to the qualification of officers, provisions with respect to the loading of ships, and things of that nature. By the statute they were made subject to revocation by order in council; and the minister will remember that there was a rather protracted discussion on the bill. Is he in a position to state which if any provisions of the Canada Shipping Act have been suspended by order in council as a result of the legislation of 1948?

Under the legislation to which my hon. friend refers, the minister has to lay on the table of the house a list of those cases in which action has been taken thereunder; and I have already done that.

Supply-Transport
I should like to ask the minister a question in reference to the gear on board vessels for the purpose of loading and unloading. Does that come under his department as subject to inspection?
Yes. There will be an item a little later on dealing with steamship inspection, and perhaps the hon. member will bring up his question then.

Under this item I should like to make a correction, offer an apology and ask a question, if I may. Last Monday, at page 2311 of Hansard, I referred to certain telegrams from officials of government departments to members of parliament, dealing with official matters, which had been sent collect. While referring to specific departments I mentioned the Department of Labour and in particular the deputy minister of labour. My good friend the Minister of Labour came over here in about ten seconds flat and in his kindly way, if I may use his phrase, told me he thought I was wrong. I looked up my files and was unable to find any telegrams sent collect by the deputy minister of labour. The telegrams in question were from the Department of External Affairs and the Department of Mines and Resources, sent to me collect on official business. May I ask the Minister of Transport, under this item which has to do with telephones, telegrams and postage, whether his department is in the habit of sending collect telegrams to hon. members in the course of handling official correspondence.
I can assure my hon. friend that we are not.

Item agreed to.
Canals service-
644.	Canals service 

 administration - further amount required, $3,000.

Has the minister had brought to his attention the fact that there is a tremendous pile of mud right at the arboretum at the experimental farm, which is very unsanitary and unsightly? It is between Dow's lake and Hartwell's locks, and I should like to know what the department is going to do about it. It will have to be taken out if you are going to put water in the canal. It is an unsightly mess and a disgrace, and I wonder if the minister would look into the matter.

It had not been brought to
my attention, but I shall see that it is brought to the attention of my officers immediately.

A couple of years ago I brought to the attention of the minister the condition of the retaining walls in a certain section of the canal, which were not in very good

shape, and tfte minister had them fixed up. If he will tell his officers to go along a bit they will find that the walls further on are also in bad shape and in need of repair, and this should be looked after also.
We have been proceeding gradually with this repair work, and it will take some time to complete it.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I would point out that this item has to do with telephones, telegrams and postage, traveling expenses, stationery and so on. Shall the item carry?

No. I should like to know whether this service is operated at a deficit or whether a profit is earned by the operation of these canals. This never appears as a deficit; it is only shown as a service. When we come to the operation of some ferries, for instance, they are always shown as a deficit. I want to know the difference between the term "service" and the word "deficit." This really should appear as a deficit in connection with the operation of the canals. Then I should like to know whether the dominion government owns the canals or whether they are owned by the provinces, and whether they are operated by the Department of Transport. I should like to have the point cleared up, to see whether there is a difference between a service and a deficit; then we can argue the other matter later.

The item we are dealing with is neither a profit nor a deficit. It is an operating expense in the amount of $3,000. That is the manner in which the accounts having to do with canals and marine services are established. They are not established on a basis of an operating agency such as a car ferry. I suppose that is what my hon. friend has in mind. So far as canals are concerned, they are the property of the dominion government, not of the province.

I just wanted to ask the minister a question about the Chignecto canal. I noticed an item the other day to the effect that the government was giving favourable consideration to investigating the possibility of constructing the Chignecto canal. I should like to hear the minister make a statement about that.

I have nothing to say on the subject. I have received a number of petitions and they are being considered at the moment. I am not in a position at this time to tell my hon. friend what will be done eventually.
Is the department giving it favourable consideration?
I am sorry I cannot tell my hon. friend that, either.

Item agreed to.
645.	Canals-operation and maintenance-further amount required, $71,470.
Will this amount appear as a capital charge also or is this for a loss on operations?
It is exclusively for operation and maintenance of the canal system. It is a further amount required.
This will be a deficit, then?
It is neither a deficit nor a surplus.
What is it?
This is an expenditure for operation and maintenance.
These are operating expenses.
That is right.

If it does not bring in revenue to the government, then it must be a deficit or a loss. The minister has not yet made this clear to me. He has not made it clear to me what is considered a deficit on services. When we come to vote 660, I suppose we will find it is termed a deficit. That is contrary to the terms under which the province of Prince Edward Island entered confederation in 1873. When we come to that item, I will argue that point.

Item agreed to.
Marine service-
646.	Construction, maintenance and supervision of aids to navigation, including salaries and allowances to lightkeepers-further amount required, $62,700.

I have two matters I want to bring to the minister's attention under this vote. One of them I have been writing to his department about for approximately four years, but the other one just came up last year. This vote of $62,700 is for the construction, maintenance and supervision of aids to navigation. This is a supplementary amount.
Some four years ago I took up with the Department of Transport the question of removing a number of old sunken hulls that are obstructing navigation in Sydney harbour. They are an eyesore. I have been following that matter up ever since. Within the last couple of months a committee was formed in the city of Sydney for the purpose of having that unsightly mess cleaned up. They wanted the Department of Transport to permit one of their dredges operating in that area either to tow these old hulls to sea or to smash them up in the harbour and allow them to
Supply-Transport
float to sea. There are certain times of the year when the dredge is laid up anyway, and it would not cost the department anything.
Oh, yes.

Well, perhaps a little bit of fuel. That is what the department was asked to do. After four long years of agitation and negotiation, the department finally sent a letter about a month ago to the effect that it could not accept any responsibility in the matter. It was a matter for the city to handle.
The city did not sink those ships in the harbour. Harbours come under the Department of Transport. In some cases these old hulls are an interference with navigation. This vote is for aids to navigation. I suggest that the department might spend $15 of the $62,000 to break up these old hulls or tow them out to sea. It is a matter of co-operation. An election may be held this year and cleaning up that mess might help you.
I now deal with the other matter. In many of the harbours, particularly where there are narrow channels, the department sets out buoys to guide ships in and out of the harbour. About four months ago a swordfish fisherman with a boat and equipment which represented about four or six thousand dollars was going out of the harbour at four o'clock in the morning. At that time it is not daylight. One of those buoys that are placed there by the Department of Transport as an aid to navigation broke loose from its moorings owing to lack of proper inspection. The fisherman ran his boat into that buoy and smashed the boat. He lost much equipment and his total loss amounted to approximately $1,500. He felt, and I agree, that he should be compensated for that loss. His boat is tied up and he is losing about a month or so of that particular season, which is a short one. He considers fifty per cent of the damage should be paid by the department.
This fisherman hired a solicitor who made application to the legal department of the Department of Transport. The legal department advised he had no claim upon the government; at least that is the letter I received from the minister.
No.
I will send it back to the minister to refresh his memory.
You need not send it back. I remember it very well and I will deal with it in a moment.

All right. This man went to a solicitor. His solicitor dealt with the legal department. The legal department informed the solicitor that there was no claim. The

Supply-Transport
solicitor for the fisherman sent all the correspondence to me and I put it in an envelope and mailed it to the minister, asking him to check on the matter. The letter the minister wrote to me merely confirmed the decision the solicitor had received from the legal department. Under those circumstances I think the government is morally and legally obligated to compensate that man because it was owing to neglect on the part of a departmental official in failing to inspect the buoy that the man suffered this loss.

Mr. Chairman, the two matters to which my hon. friend has made reference are not as easily disposed of as he implies. With reference to the first matter, may I say that no one detests sunken craft more than I do when I see them in our rivers and harbours. It is not as easy to dispose of them as the member believes. He seems to be under the impression that all one needs to do is to tow them out into the channel and dispose of them without more ado.
I do not know the particular facts to which he refers, but I do know the general picture in the department. It is as follows: Very often these craft are sunk by people who have no further use for them. Then these people go into bankruptcy. Under the act we are required to notify them to remove the craft. When they do not remove the craft, then we have to take action and very often the cost is high.
My hon. friend complains about what is happening in his constituency. I can tell him what is happening in my own constituency and in the adjoining constituency of Glengarry. A large number of craft have been lying there for at least twenty years because the owners will not remove them or have gone out of business, cannot be found, or have gone into receivership. There are so many matters that come into the picture, it is not so easy to dispose of these craft as one would imagine. However, I can assure the hon. gentleman that the officers of the Department of Transport are extremely anxious to get rid of these craft wherever it is possible. There are some cases where it can be done and it is done.
With regard to the buoy that was displaced by a storm, there are legal officers in the Department of Transport and the Department of Justice also advises the other departments of government. As a matter of fact we accept the advice of the Department of Justice. In this case, that department ruled that the moving of the buoy was an act of God and that there was no legal liability on the Department of Transport.
There is not much justice there. tMr. Gillis.]

So I wrote to my hon. friend stating that I was extremely sorry-I am sure I must have told him that-that under the circumstances there was nothing I could do, since there was no legal responsibility. I wish there were some way in which I could help my hon. friend, but legally there is not.

I have heard everybody else blamed, but now we are getting around to having it blamed on God. I think there is something that can be done. I agree that-many of the harbours across Canada have been cluttered up with these ships for twenty years, simply because you have not the kind of legislation which permits you to clean them up. In this particular case the owners of these hulls had been canvassed by a committee from the city council and they said that as far as they were concerned they had no interest in them. They said, "Do what you like with them." That rules out the technicality that the owner is responsible or that legal action must be taken to have them removed. Why do you not change the act and notify anyone in this country who has that kind of mess in any harbour that, if within thirty days he does not do something about it, you will clean it up yourself? You can do that. It is a matter of amending the legislation.
In the other case, I do not know who made the decision but I do not think there is any justice. If the department is responsible for placing the buoy there as an aid to navigation, then there certainly should be some inspection. On the night that buoy went adrift, there was little disturbance in the ocean, as I remember it, because I happened to be at home at the time. I think myself it just lay there for so long without anyone looking after it that whatever was holding it there rusted and rotted away and it went adrift.
This man I know was claiming only half the damage he suffered to his boat and gear. In addition to that, he lost that swordfishing season, which meant perhaps $4,000, $5,000 or $6,000 to him. All he was asking for was enough to put that boat back in shape. This is his means of livelihood, I believe the minister should yet reconsider the matter. I can quite understand that an official of the Department of Justice who perhaps has resided here all his life, who has had little to do with the fishing industry and has no conception of it, might, on the basis of a law passed fifty years ago, make a decision that certainly has no application to the kind of thing that I am talking about. I suggest that he might take a look at the matter again and try to persuade whoever made the decision that, though it may

be in keeping with a law written long ago, it is unjust under present conditions. I know the minister will do that, and I hope that I will hear from him shortly to the effect that those two things are cleared up.

It is not a question of the law written thirty years ago; it is a question of the law as it exists today.
But you have never changed it for thirty years.

Every time I listen to a discussion concerning the Department of Transport on matters dealing with lighthouse keepers, buoys and so on I notice that we always come back to what the lawyers say about it. My belief with regard to this item is that it concerns a government-owned

service and not a government enterprise, and for that reason it should not appear here as if it were chargeable against Prince Edward Island as a deficit. In order to prove to the minister that this is a service I am going to quote from an order in council passed at the court of Windsor on June 26, 1873, which reads:
That the dominion government shall assume and defray all the charges for the following services, viz.:-
Efficient steam service for the conveyance of mails and passengers, to be established and maintained between the island and the mainland of the dominion, winter and summer, thus placing the island in continuous communication with the Intercolonial railway and the railway system of the dominion . . .
And such other charges as may be incident to and connected with the services which by the British North America Act, 1867, appertain to the general government, and as are or may be allowed to the other provinces.
I cannot see why each year this should appear as a deficit. It is purely a service under a contract entered into in 1873, so why should it appear in the public accounts as a deficit? If it is not a deficit in the case of the canals, for the same kind of service, why should it be a deficit in the case of ferry boats?

I do not want to get into an argument with my hon. friend, who raises this question every year. The reason it is set out this way is that it has been so recommended by the Duncan commission. At page 28 the report of that commission states:
We further recommend that, so far as the ferry boat service is concerned, it should not be run as part of the railway operations, but should be run by the railway administration under separate account for the department.
And the recommendation goes on:
We feel that, by reason of its association with railway accounts, this service does not get the attention it should receive.
Because the Duncan commission felt that way about it, the department has always included a separate item set out in that manner, in order to establish a difference between the Prince Edward Island car ferry and other services of the Department of Transport. The reason the word "deficit" is used in this appropriation is that the operating revenues of the service are applied against the operating expenses, and the deficiency is correctly termed a deficit. I wish I could meet the request of my hon. friend. He brought up the matter last year; he brought it up in the committee on railways and shipping, where he cross-examined the railway witnesses, and they gave him the answer I am giving now. Until there is some better reason, it strikes me the item should remain as it is.
