Supply-Trade and Commerce Mr. Howe: Mr. Chairman, this item is for the purchase of two materials only; one is tin and the other is antimony. Tin is under international allocation. Quantities have been allocated to Canada from year to year. The situation in Malaya, which is the principal source of tin, is disturbed. At the end of 1948 it was found that Canada had not taken up its full allocation of tin for the year.
The munitions advisory board, a board of businessmen with some experience in military supply matters, examined the situation and strongly recommended to the government that it should take up the balance of its allocation for 1948 as a precautionary measure. The provisions of the international agreement are that if allocations are not taken up in any year future allocations may be cut back to the amount actually taken. That was thought to be a dangerous situation; it was felt that prices are likely to advance rather than decline. The world situation is tight. All in all, the munitions advisory board recommended that we take up this allocation, and that has carried the judgment of the experts in my own department. The result is that we have obtained authority from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) to purchase tin in the amount indicated.
Does this mean we shall have to take up our allocation each year if we do not use it?

No; we regard the present stockpile as adequate. If conditions ease we may sell out the stockpile at any time. At the moment we could do so at a profit.
The other provision concerned a certain quantity of antimony. One of the principal sources of this material is China. We have placed an order with the Chinese government for a certain quantity of antimony. It has not yet been delivered, but the provision in the estimates is for the payment thereof.
Will the minister explain the method by which these purchases are made, and more particularly the authority under which purchases of these strategic materials are made by the government?

Payment was by an advance from the treasury which is made under the authority of an order in council. We are now asking for the appropriation of the funds required to make the purchase. The purchase was under an international allocation. Certain quantities of the material were allocated to us and that was purchased from these sources of supply which are the sources for any Canadian purchaser who buys under allocation.

Would it not be wise to have some statutory provision for the purchase of these strategic materials? Apparently there is to be quite a bit of that done from now on,


and it would seem to be advisable to have the procedure for doing it set out; to have measures enacted for authorizing the payment by the government.

It is not thought that we need go beyond these two materials. The other recommendation had to do with quartz crystals, which come chiefly from Brazil. The department examined the quartz crystal situation and it is believed supplies are adequate to protect any situation that is likely to arise. Those are the three recommendations that were made.
Canada is a surplus country in most of the critical materials. For example, we are surplus in copper, zinc, lead, tungsten and a number of other metals. There is not much use in stockpiling materials we have in abundance. I think, therefore, that no general provision is required. There will be a small provision in the main estimates to take care of this shipment of antimony which has not yet arrived, there will be a small provision either in the main estimates, or in the supplementary estimates.
Item agreed to.
627. Canadian government travel bureau-to assist in promoting the tourist business in Canada-provided in main estimates under Trade and Commerce -further amount required, $87,000.

I see the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters) is not present. Before this item is passed, I wonder whether the minister would consider giving the house a statement of policy with respect to the tourist industry? Perhaps there are other items that might be considered in the meantime.

Mr. Chairman, if I might speak as acting minister, these are the last of the further supplementary estimates. It is desirable to have these dealt with in another place and to get the final consent of the crown before tomorrow night. We have passed the end of the fiscal year to which these apply. I will undertake, therefore, to deal with any questions my hon. friend may have in mind.

I was wondering, then, if the minister would be kind enough, and I have no doubt he would, to give the house a statement of government policy with respect to the tourist industry. We are all aware that for several years there has not been a statement of policy in respect to this industry which we believe is of vital importance to our economy.
This travel bureau has, I think, been under ten different ministries since 1934. During the life of this parliament it has been, I

believe, under four different ministries. To my knowledge, we have not had what I think we are entitled to, that is an announcement as to how the government intends to proceed to develop this industry. We know some advertising is being done. For instance, we understand it is the intention of the bureau to open film libraries in the United States. I believe the minister will agree with me that this project is worthy of a great deal more consideration than it has apparently received.
For instance, I should like to know if the ministry really has in mind the opening of these film libraries. Where are the films to be taken? Are they to be taken in the various provinces? Is the advertising in the various publications to be allocated according to the areas from which the greatest number would come? I contend that this is sales advertising, Mr. Chairman. There is one point I should like to emphasize tonight, in view of the fact there is a possibility these film libraries might be opened up. On the staff of each of the libraries in these cities there should be a competent person who could give a talk on certain areas in Canada. There might be thirty or forty of these libraries throughout the United States.
There are other questions with respect to advertising to which I believe we are entitled to have answers. Quite candidly, I say to the minister that this year I believe the advertising has been much more appropriate than it has been in the past. I wonder if the minister could answer these questions now, so that we could make some progress. I do not wish to delay the house, but perhaps we could finish this item in a very few minutes.

Mr. Chairman, the federal tourist bureau is really a co-ordinating agency for other tourist activities in Canada. Every province in Canada has its own tourist agency which handles advertising having to do with the attractions of that province. Our railways and shipping companies also have tourist publicity relating to their own particular resorts. The federal tourist bureau handles advertising on a national scale. In other words, it advertises all of Canada. The inquiries that come to it are usually sent to other agencies to be dealt with. If someone is interested in a visit to Ontario, the tourist department of the government of Ontario is advised, and so on. If he wants a trip down the St. Lawrence, the proper travel agency there is advised. The advertising has been stepped up from year to year. I was minister in charge of this department from 1935 to 1939, and the appropriations of those days were less than half the present one. I think the quality of the advertising has also been
Supply-Reconstruction and Supply improved as a result of experience as to the type of advertising that interests our friends to the south.
Then there are other activities of the department. Recently there has been wide distribution in the United States of films showing Canadian recreational opportunities. This work has been carried on by a group of United States moving picture companies which have banded together in what is called the Canadian co-operative project; and without expenditure of any funds on the part of Canada, those interested in the project have worked with this bureau to choose films and to make in Canada films that could be shown in the United States and which would have entertainment appeal as well as value in advertising Canada.
As to film libraries, I presume my hon. friend refers to the activities of the film board. Is that so?
Yes.

I know of no activities of the travel bureau having to do with film libraries in the United States, but perhaps I am out of date. I think the Minister of Finance is more familiar with that matter. He says he knows about the film board. I think he can perhaps answer my hon. friend's question on the next item which has to do with the film board. I may say that this particular $87,000 arises through a special advertising effort made in connection with Canada's winter resorts. The improvement in our dollar balance arising out of the tourist traffic last summer was such that it was felt that some special advertising was warranted to help us bring in United States dollars during the winter season.

When in February I spoke in the house on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I urged the government to consider setting up a standing committee to co-operate and work with the minister to develop this industry which to me is highly important. I said-and I think most hon. members will agree-that this tourist bureau had been treated as an adjunct. I was sincere when I spoke the other night on this industry. As I see it, we should be developing a billion dollar industry. I do not think any hon. member in this house, under these conditions and in these times, is satisfied with a ten per cent increase per year in our tourist industry. It is not enough. I do not think that the industry has received from the government the attention that it warrants.
When I suggested the committee, I felt that this industry should be dealt with on a businesslike basis. It did not make any difference

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply to us whether the committee was composed of six from the government benches or seventy per cent and thirty per cent from the opposition. It would not make any difference. I think there are enough members in this House of Commons, keenly interested in this tourist industry, who are only too anxious and willing to have this committee set up, to work together and really develop the tourist industry. Can the minister give to the committee any information with respect to that request? I am satisfied that if the committee were set up after Easter we would be able to get the experts in advertising and in sales from companies who have made a success of their own development and business, and that a great deal of useful information could be obtained as a basis for bringing this industry up to the level which it really demands. Can the minister make a statement with regard to that matter?
With respect to libraries, I may have been a little bit presumptuous. I understood that some of the provinces have small film libraries here and there in many parts of the United States, and that is the country from which we expect to get the much-needed United States dollars. Somehow or other I had the idea that it was the intention of this government to open up, under this travel bureau, film libraries in the United States. My point was this. I think it is most advisable that such action be taken. I think the provinces themselves should suggest the films that could be taken and these would be stored in those libraries.
But to me the most important part of the question is selling the tourist industry to these people. There is no use in having the films in the libraries if they are not going to be shown. Our tourist business comes to this country through people who may have been here for a week, two weeks or a month, as the case may be. They are ambassadors. We are simply selling good will. The more of those whom we can approach, either by having them come here or by showing them what we have to offer, the better it will be, because that is where our market will be. Even at the present level of our income from the tourist business, I think that this country can increase it not only ten per cent but a great deal more. I think our aim should be at least twenty-five per cent per year. According to the figures which I have given before, and of which the house is fully aware, even then we would not be getting our share of what we could rightly claim of the amount spent by Americans on vacation.
Can the minister tell us whether or not they would seriously consider that suggestion? I think it is important that we have men who are willing and able to co-operate


with the minister for the sole purpose of developing this most important industry.

I fully agree with my hon. friend as to the importance of the industry. I also fully agree with him as to the objectives of this branch of the government. As to the appointment of a committee, he will appreciate the fact that all I can do is to call his remarks to the attention of my colleague, and ask him to give the matter his careful consideration.

Item agreed to.
General-
628. National film board, Including the motion picture bureau-provided in main estimates under national revenue-distribution of films-further amount required, $20,000.
I should like to make a few remarks on this item and to ask a few questions of the Minister of Finance, who says he knows all the answers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not all the answers.

Rather, the Minister of Trade and Commerce said he knew the answers. The film board is much like the tourist bureau. It has been under a great number of ministers. The first minister, Mr. Euler, when he was setting up that board, said there would be only one paid official and that they were not setting up the board in order to create jobs. But at the present time there are almost six hundred employees in there, although that is not the number who were in there a few years ago. There were over seven hundred in there a few years ago. I have criticized the national film board for some years. I am glad I have done so for this reason. There is a definite improvement in the national film board pictures, although I must say that the film the national film board took of the opening of parliament is a disgrace to any organization.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I thought it was wonderful.
I saw it last night.
They must have had the minister's face in focus. They did not have anybody else's in focus.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Don't blame the film board for the minister's face.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are judges of male beauty, I think.
There is a lot of room for improvement yet.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: In the minister's face?

I hope the minister does not take that personally. I did not mean his face,
I meant the national film board.

The hon. member who has just taken his seat spoke about the tourist industry. I agree with him that films should be used in the United States for advertising, but in the United States the national film board should not be the agency for distributing them. That should be left with the tourist bureau, which has men who are trained for that purpose. As the hon. gentleman said, the films should be under the supervision of the different provinces in co-operation with the tourist bureau.
This item deals with distribution of films, and I shall deal entirely with that. It calls for $20,000 in addition to what was voted last year. Last year the estimate for distribution amounted to $57,826. In his report Mr. Sellar, the Auditor General, brought to light the fact that the distribution was not carried on the way it should be. There are phantom showings of the national film board pictures and that is under distribution. Some of the men who are in the employ of the national film board do not carry out their duties. They say that they have shown films here, there and in the other place and they have not done so.
Mention has been made of distribution in the United States. I should like to ask the minister to make a note of this question and answer it when I am through. I understand that a year ago the film board had a man in Chicago whose name was Wesley Green. He was in the office of the national film board and walked out with $7,000 worth of films which, according to my information, have never been returned to the board. I should like to know whether that is correct or not.
I shall read a list of the bureaux or offices of the national film board outside of Canada. According to a return tabled in answer to a question of mine on February 23 of this year, the national film board has one office in Chicago, one in London, England, one in New York and one in Mexico. According to the return the Mexico office shows only two employees, but the Toronto Star Weekly or the Saturday Night of a month or so ago showed a picture of the receptionist of the national film board's Mexico office sunning herself on a beach in Mexico.
It might have been a Wednesday afternoon.

I object to the national film board offices distributing films in the United States, and also to the way they are carrying on business. I hold in my hand a sheet from a film magazine which contains an advertisement of the national film board of Canada, 620 Fifth avenue, New York City, and 400 West Madison street, Chicago, Illinois. This
7, 1949	2453
Supply-Reconstruction and Supply is not an advertisement for tourists to come to Canada. What does it say? It says:
The answer to this question may necessitate reviewing his life from birth . . .
Why won't Tommy eat?
16 mm sound-2 reels-colour National film board of Canada
Is that going to help Canada's trade? Is that going to help the tourist industry? I think it is an absolute disgrace. This advertisement was brought to my attention by at least fifty people across Canada and the United States.
I have a letter from the director of administration of the library of congress of the United States. I asked him a question regarding the distribution and the set-up of the film board in the United States, and this is what he has to say:
The committee desires that before another budget is presented the whole matter be restudied with a view to (1) determining the extent to which it is practicable for the government to carry on this kind of activity, and (2) whether or not the library of congress is the logical agency to administer if it is determined that the expenditure of public funds for such a purpose is necessary.
I understand that the whole film set-up of the United States is being liquidated at the present time in order that they may start off anew and see what can be done. That is something which should be done here.
Carried.

I heard an hon. member say "carried". I do not know who it was, but I am not going to hurry, and I shall tell the committee why. Last year the estimates for the national film board were not brought down until about eleven o'clock on the last night the house sat. In 1947 the same thing happened; therefore I am going to take my time no matter what the hon. member may say.
Take your time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Don't hurry at all.
Very interesting.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are following you with bated breath.

This is one thing that has been brought to my attention by commercial photographers across Canada. In one department I believe there is an expenditure of some $121,000 for making just ordinary still pictures. Commercial photographers wonder why employees of the national film board are allowed to sell films or pictures and have their own names on them. I am going to mention the names of two employees. One is George Hunter and the other Frank Royal. One picture was taken down in Mexico and was shown here not long ago. It was in one
2454	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Supply-Reconstruction and Supply of the magazines in the United States, and evidently the New York office or the Chicago office sold to some firm in the United States a series called: "Let's all sing together." Some firm in the United States is advertising these films which were made by the national film board. I do not believe that that should be done. The board was not set up to sell films to other countries, unless they are films for trade purposes or films to advertise our industry.
I asked what the traveling, hotel and meals expenses were for the national film board during 1948 and was told that the hotels, meals and taxi expenses amounted to $89,000. The amount for transportation is $100,283.79, for entertainment $1,550.98, and for moving expenses $1,840.20.
Another question I should like to ask arises from the fact that the Ottawa Journal of this evening states "Carr Tells of '45 Negotiations With Liberals." It states that Mr. Paul Martin and Mr. Alan McLean were interviewed. I wonder if the McLean who is director of the national film board is a brother of this McLean, who is national organizer for the Liberal party.
Here is an advertisement in the magazine called "Photography" entitled Let's All Sing Together, and which gives a list of all the productions of the national film board. But this appears as an advertisement of Library Films Incorporated of New York.
The national film board have been taking pictures right across the country, some of which are good and some not so good. It was brought to my attention from New Brunswick that the film board went to a point called Hartman's pool-and the Minister of Fisheries will know where that is. The film board paid men to go there and jig for salmon. That is a procedure of gaffing them-and one which is entirely against the law. Yet the board has done that in other places. I wonder if there should not be some restrictions against that outfit for doing things for which the ordinary man would be arrested?
Jigging them is not gaffing them.
What is jigging?
Catching them on the hook without bait on it.
But that is the same thing.
A gaff is a long pole with a sharp end on it. It is a different operation altogether.
They used three-pronged hooks without any bait on them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is spearing them.
They yank those up and down, which is against the law. Yet the national film board were allowed to do this, and I say it is entirely wrong.
It was codfish you saw, not salmon.

It was salmon they were after; it was salmon they caught; it was salmon they took pictures of. The national film board made a picture called People Between, and stated that it was made for UNRRA. This picture was taken in China. Mr. Grant McLean went there to take it; but as it was thought that it might offend Chiang Kai-shek's government the Department of External Affairs said it should not be shown in Canada. They are trying to sell that picture. I would ask the minister to comment upon that.
In the taking of that picture alone there were traveling expenses of over $879.50 paid by the national film board to save time through returning cameramen by air to London.
I have seen some pictures turned out by the national film board which I have felt are not up to snuff, and could be much better. In this connection I would ask whether we have not some good camera directors in Canada? If so, why was it necessary for the board to go to the United States and employ men there?
An item in another issue of "Photography" states:
Back from a flying trip to the Northwest Territories and into the Arctic Circle directing motion picture newsreels and stills for the national film board, Canadian government agency, is Hamilton Wright, Jr., of New York city. Wright left San Juan, Puerto Rico, early in February at 80 above zero. Fifty-one hours later, including a stop-over in New York, he arrived at The Pas.
Why is it that we have to engage American camera directors?
Mention was made of the stills department.
I know that every commercial photographer across Canada feels as I do in this matter, because I have had letters from over five hundred of them, and also from press photographers, objecting to the stills department which last year took 167,854 photographs, at a rate of more than 500 a day. They are selling these in competition with the ordinary man who pays taxes to the Minister of Finance. I say that is unfair competition, and should be stopped.
There is the further fact that estimates of the national film board are not correct estimates. In those estimates there should be reflected the fact that last year the Department of Public Works paid out, so far as I can learn, $34,000 on new improvements in

the twelve buildings occupied here in Ottawa by the national film board. Besides that the Department of Public Works paid for all telephone, operating and building expenses. If the film board were under proper direction and management it could be made to operate in the best interests of the people.
We have film councils right across Canada, all of which are doing good work. But in many instances they have had to buy or rent films from other agencies to show to the people, despite the fact that the national film board has distributors and other men who go around the country showing films. I would ask the minister to give me an answer to my questions.

Mr. Chairman, notwithstanding all the bad things of which the film board is supposed to be guilty, I know one good thing it does. It allows us to have its films at Fort William on trust. I have enjoyed hour after hour seeing on film the great beauties to be seen in Canada. These are the tourist attractions which show our beautiful caves, surrounded by large stones which have an appeal for the tourists who come here from the United States, and who certainly have their eyes opened when they see the films turned out by the national film board.
Just a moment. I hope the hon. member does not think I am saying anything against the film board.
Oh, oh.
I criticize it only so that it may be better. I have not said that pictures taken across the country have not been good. Perhaps the films the hon. member saw were taken by some other organization.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have not extensive knowledge of the affairs of the national film board. Unfortunately the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply had an engagement of long standing to address the Ontario Liberal Association, and could not be here this evening.
I have come prepared to answer questions with respect to this particular item, but I am afraid I cannot deal with questions relating to the general administration of the film board, as they have been set out by the hon. member for Peterborough West. I shall see however that those questions are brought to the attention of the minister who, I have no doubt, will answer them when the main estimates of the film board are before the committee.
This estimate is for an additional $20,000 for international distribution of national films through Canadian missions abroad. In 1947-48 the estimate was for $i?6,000. Trea-
7, 1949	2455
Supply-Reconstruction and Supply sury board was taking a strict view of expenditures of the film board in 1948, and the amount was cut down to $76,000. It was found from experience that that was too drastic and this $20,000 is required to provide the distribution which it is felt is necessary for these films in our missions abroad.
Does the minister think that the national film board should carry on with its stills departments? Would that be part of their distribution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not given that question any consideration. I have seen some splendid pictures which they have taken of members of parliament.
Do you think that pictures of members of parliament are an asset?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that those I have seen are quite good.

In view of the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, could the Minister of Finance answer my inquiry regarding film depots in the United States and whether the films would be made by the film board?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not in position to make a statement. I listened to what my hon. friend said and if my colleague brings in an estimate to treasury board for that purpose it will receive sympathetic consideration.
Item agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again this day.
Progress reported.

speechtext:
I understand that it is the desire of most hon. members to dispose of these estimates. If that is so I would move:
That this house do sit this day beyond the hour of ten-thirty p.m.

speechtext: Can there not be some understanding as to how long we will sit?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I understand that there is only one item left and I would hope that it would not be very long.

expects that, because we want it to be short, commitments will be made by the minister, I must say at once that that is not likely. I do not think that any member of the house would wish to sit very long. If it seems that

Supply-Health and Welfare a debate is developing that will take a long time I think it could be understood that we will move to adjourn both the debate and the house.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

I am not going to object.

speechtext: I think it should be understood that if a situation develops which would take us beyond a reasonable hour both the debate and the house should be adjourned. In view of the lateness of the hour I shall speak only for a few minutes although I regret that the government has seen fit not to follow through with the items in their regular order but to skip this item and then bring it on at the last. In the last few days there has been an important development in the field of old age pensions. I refer to the announcement by the government of Ontario that believing that the basic-

I believe, and the Progressive Conservative party believes, the time has come to increase that basic old age pension. I suggest it should be raised to at least $40 per month, and I propose to point out to the committee three reasons why I believe that should be done. The first is that the basic pension was set by the present government at $30 a month in 1947, two years ago. It was inadequate at that time, as was admitted by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. If hon. members will refer to page 4744 of Hansard, for that session they will find that the minister gave this answer on being questioned about the amount of $30:
I do not say, and no one says, that $30 a month is enough for a person to live on.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The first argument I was putting forward in support of the increase in the basic pension to at least $40 a month was that two years ago the minister himself admitted that $30 a month was inadequate for a person to live on. The cost of living index for Canada on June 1, 1947, stood at 134.9 as compared with the years 1935-39. On March 1, 1949, the index had gone up over 24 points, to 159.2. So if $30 was inadequate in 1947 it is very much more inadequate in 1949. The second argument I submit is that last year the war veterans' allowance was fixed by the dominion government at $40 per month. In that case the veteran is the charge of the dominion government alone. This year the war veterans' allowance for a single man may be increased from $40 to $50.

The action of another department of this government clearly shows that that department at least considers that $40 is a basic payment and is willing to pay an additional $10 per month.

speechtext:
The third argument I wish to place before the house is that the money required to pay this increased basic pension would, of course, have to be paid by the Canadian people. They have shown that they are in favour of an increase in the amount paid. On February 23,	1949, a
Gallup poll reported on this question of the amount people thought should be paid by way of old age pensions. The report reads:
The old age pension rate issue holds keen interest amongst Canadian voters, the great majority of whom would favour notably higher benefits.
At another point the article reads:
The amounts advocated in the most recent study were: $20 or less, one per cent; $21 to $30, 4 per cent;-
-so that at the present time the government is only meeting the wishes of 5 per cent of the people queried in this poll.
$31 to $40, 11 per cent; $41 to $50, 29 per cent; $51 to $60, 17 per cent; $61 to $99, 21 per cent; $100 or over, 9 per cent; no suggestion offered, 8 per cent.
This poll virtually indicates that the vast majority of the people of Canada believe the old age pension should be increased. They are taking into consideration of course the amounts actually received which, in some provinces, are over $30 at the present time.
These senior citizens of Canada and our blind citizens are in a trapped group. They can secure no increase in their wages. They are on a fixed income. The cost of their living has gone up. I know in my own city of Vancouver many of them are in a tragic position. They are not given any help at all by the present budget. They seem to be the forgotten men and women of Canada, in these days of huge national income and of large surpluses. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that is not good enough for Canada in this year 1949. I urge that the government at this session raise the basic pension to at least $40.
With these old people time is of great importance. A year from now many of them will have passed away. They are always faced with that time element. I do urge the government to increase the basic pension at this session to at least $40 per month. I point out that it had better act quickly because if it does not act at this session, the new Progressive Conservative government will put through this increase.

This is a debatable motion, even though the minister has risen to try to cut off debate.

Supply-Ways and Means Mr. Abbott: We are in committee.

Yes, we are in committee, but the motion is a debatable one. The amendment is debatable because the amendment now is that the amount of the estimate be reduced by a certain sum of money, namely, some $5,000.
Those of us who believe that all that is necessary should be given to the department to deal with pensions for the blind and for old age pensioners are not in favour of reducing the amount by $1 when it is to be used for that particular purpose. I am sorry the minister used the method that he adopted tonight in stopping the debate, because one hon. gentleman had been allowed to proceed with this matter, and particularly when the members of the house were good enough, shall I say, to agree to the suggestion that we should sit beyond the hour of adjournment.
The minister rose in his place and appeared to be quite annoyed at any criticism being leveled at the department in connection with old age pensions. Let me point out to him that the C.C.F. group in this house two years ago urged that the basic pension should be raised to $50 a month, and that motion was ruled out of order at the time. What I am going to point out is this. As the hon. member for Vancouver South has stated, in those two years the cost of living has risen by twenty-four points. As the controls have been removed, the cost of living has risen. The result is that the old age pensioners, who were to get $30 a month two years ago, are today getting the equivalent in purchasing power of $22.50 per month, which means a considerable reduction in their standard of living.
I think the government owes it to the house and to the country to grant a substantial increase in pensions to the old age pensioners and to the blind in this country.
I have always believed that the pensions should be uniform across the country and that the whole amount should be paid from the federal treasury so that there would not be this competition among the provinces, which I think is bad for the old age pensioners, for the provinces and for the general public. I am urging that the government take the opportunity of announcing to the people of this country that the old age pension will be raised so that at least the standard of living, such as it was, will be restored.
In this country where we have had such large budgetary surpluses I think that could well be done. Our senior citizens, as they are called nowadays, and the persons who are blind are entitled to something better than 
they are getting. I am sorry the minister chose the method he did of ending the debate tonight. I am not going to say any more at this stage, because I know that the house desires to go through with the arrangements that have been made. I did want to join with others, however, in making this protest against the manner in which the debate was closed tonight.

In the public accounts there are listed certain miscellaneous grants to various blind organizations: The Canadian National Institute for the Blind, L'Association Canadienne Francaise des Aveugles, L'lnstitut Nazareth de Montreal and the Montreal Association for the Blind; and the Canadian Federation of the Blind has presented to all political parties in this house this petition which I will read so that it will be on the record:
Whereas the Canadian Federation of the Blind is an organization operating throughout Canada with a federal charter obtained in 1928, and duly recognized by the Secretary of State, and is directed by sightless people with the assistance of sighted associate members for the promotion and protection of the interests of the blind, and
Whereas our national executive is of the opinion that being a democratic organization of the blind we are in the best position to understand and advise in matters pertaining to the blind and to give the most effective administration in their interests.

In this case.
-to consider the advisability of proposing legislation which will include the Canadian Federation of the Blind as a major agency in blind welfare work throughout the dominion, and that the Canadian Federation of the Blind be given an appropriation from the federal treasury.

I support that resolution; and I should like to have the Minister of National Health and Welfare consider this petition-that is, for distribution of federal funds to the various blind welfare organizations throughout Canada-on the same basis on which it is making contributions to the four associations that I previously mentioned.
